----------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the API documentation for the perfinpy library.
----------------------------------------------------------------------


## Income

Foundations. Functions from the Income chapter.


wealth_formula(median_income: 'ArrayLike', savings_rate: 'ArrayLike', annual_return: 'ArrayLike', years: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Wealth from saving part of an income every year.

The future value of saving `median_income * savings_rate` at the end of
each year (contributions plus growth). From the
[Income](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/income.html) chapter.

Parameters
----------
median_income
    Yearly income.
savings_rate
    Share of income saved, as a decimal.
annual_return
    Yearly return, as a decimal. A 0% return gives the sum of the
    contributions.
years
    Number of years.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Ending balances.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

See Also
--------
raise_invested_value : Monthly version for investing part of a raise.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import wealth_formula
>>> # $45,000 income, 20% saved, 7% return, 30 years
>>> wealth_formula(45000, savings_rate=0.20, annual_return=0.07, years=30)
850147.07

fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs: 'ArrayLike', take_home: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Fixed costs as a percent of take home pay.

From the [Income](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/income.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
fixed_costs
    Monthly fixed costs (rent, insurance, loan payments).
take_home
    Monthly take home pay. Must be greater than 0.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Percentages (`56.25` is 56.25%).

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values, or `take_home` is not
    greater than 0.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import fixed_cost_ratio
>>> fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs=1800, take_home=3200)
56.25

raise_invested_value(monthly_raise: 'ArrayLike', invest_share: 'ArrayLike', rate: 'ArrayLike', years: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Future value of investing part of a raise.

Invests `monthly_raise * invest_share` every month, compounded monthly.
From the [Income](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/income.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
monthly_raise
    Monthly increase in take home pay.
invest_share
    Share of the raise invested, as a decimal.
rate
    Yearly return, as a decimal.
years
    Number of years.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Ending balances.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

See Also
--------
wealth_formula : Yearly version for saving part of an income.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import raise_invested_value
>>> # invest half of a $200/month raise at 7% for 30 years
>>> raise_invested_value(200, invest_share=0.5, rate=0.07, years=30)
121997.09


## Tracking Spending

Foundations. Functions from the Tracking Spending chapter.


apply_rules(df: 'pl.DataFrame', rules: 'pl.DataFrame') -> 'pl.DataFrame'

Categorize transactions with keyword rules.

Each row of `rules` holds a regular expression (`Pattern`) and the
`Category` it assigns. Rules are tried in order and the first match wins;
matching ignores case. Descriptions that match no rule get `"Other"`.
From the [Tracking Spending](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/tracking_spending.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
df
    Transactions with a string `Description` column.
rules
    Rules with string `Pattern` and `Category` columns.

Returns
-------
polars.DataFrame
    `df` with a `Category` column added (or replaced).

Raises
------
TypeError
    If `df` or `rules` is not a polars DataFrame.
ValueError
    If a required column is missing.

Examples
--------
>>> import polars as pl
>>> from perfinpy import apply_rules
>>> transactions = pl.DataFrame(
...     {"Description": ["SAFEWAY #123", "NETFLIX.COM", "ATM FEE"]}
... )
>>> rules = pl.DataFrame(
...     {"Pattern": ["safeway", "netflix"],
...      "Category": ["Groceries", "Subscriptions"]}
... )
>>> apply_rules(transactions, rules)["Category"].to_list()
['Groceries', 'Subscriptions', 'Other']

subscription_opportunity_cost(monthly_cost: 'ArrayLike', years: 'ArrayLike', rate: 'ArrayLike' = 0.07) -> 'Numeric'

What a subscription would grow to if invested instead.

Treats the yearly cost (`monthly_cost * 12`) as a contribution made at
the end of each year and grows it at `rate`. From the
[Tracking Spending](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/tracking_spending.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
monthly_cost
    Monthly subscription price.
years
    Number of years.
rate
    Yearly return, as a decimal. Defaults to 0.07.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Future values.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import subscription_opportunity_cost
>>> # $15/month for 30 years at 7%
>>> subscription_opportunity_cost(monthly_cost=15, years=30)
17002.94


## Budgeting

Foundations. Functions from the Budgeting chapter.


percent_of_income(expense: 'ArrayLike', income: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

An expense as a percent of income.

`expense` and `income` must cover the same period. From the
[Budgeting](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/budgeting.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
expense
    Amount spent.
income
    Income for the same period. Must be greater than 0.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Percentages (`30` is 30%).

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values, or `income` is not greater
    than 0.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import percent_of_income
>>> percent_of_income(expense=1500, income=5000)
30.0

to_annual(amount: 'ArrayLike', period: "Literal['daily', 'weekly', 'monthly']" = 'daily') -> 'Numeric'

Convert a daily, weekly, or monthly amount to a yearly amount.

Uses 365 days, 52 weeks, and 12 months per year. From the
[Budgeting](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/budgeting.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
amount
    Amount per `period`.
period
    One of `"daily"`, `"weekly"`, or `"monthly"`.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Yearly amounts.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If `amount` is not numeric.
ValueError
    If `amount` contains missing values, or `period` is not one of the
    choices.

See Also
--------
to_monthly : Convert to a monthly amount.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import to_annual
>>> # $5 a day coffee
>>> to_annual(amount=5, period="daily")
1825.0

to_monthly(amount: 'ArrayLike', period: "Literal['daily', 'weekly', 'annual']" = 'daily') -> 'Numeric'

Convert a daily, weekly, or yearly amount to a monthly amount.

Uses the book's rounded factors: 30.44 days and 4.33 weeks per month, so
a round trip through `to_annual()` drifts slightly. From the
[Budgeting](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/budgeting.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
amount
    Amount per `period`.
period
    One of `"daily"`, `"weekly"`, or `"annual"`.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Monthly amounts.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If `amount` is not numeric.
ValueError
    If `amount` contains missing values, or `period` is not one of the
    choices.

See Also
--------
to_annual : Convert to a yearly amount.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import to_monthly
>>> # $150 a week in groceries
>>> to_monthly(amount=150, period="weekly")
649.5

opportunity_cost(amount: 'ArrayLike', rate: 'ArrayLike', years: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

What an amount could grow to if invested instead of spent.

Compounds `amount` once a year at `rate`. From the
[Budgeting](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/budgeting.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
amount
    Amount spent today.
rate
    Yearly return, as a decimal.
years
    Number of years.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Future values.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import opportunity_cost
>>> # $25,000 saved on a car, invested at 7% for 30 years
>>> opportunity_cost(amount=25000, rate=0.07, years=30)
190306.37

months_to_break_even(upfront_cost: 'ArrayLike', monthly_savings: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Months until monthly savings cover an upfront cost.

The result is not rounded. From the
[Budgeting](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/budgeting.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
upfront_cost
    Cost paid today.
monthly_savings
    Amount saved each month. Must be greater than 0.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Months.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values, or `monthly_savings` is not
    greater than 0.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import months_to_break_even
>>> # $500 membership that saves $60 a month
>>> months_to_break_even(upfront_cost=500, monthly_savings=60)
8.33


## Managing Debt

Foundations. Functions from the Managing Debt chapter.


apr_to_apy(apr: 'ArrayLike', periods_per_year: 'ArrayLike' = 365) -> 'Numeric'

Convert an APR to an annual percentage yield (APY).

From the [Managing Debt](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/managing_debt.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
apr
    Annual percentage rate, as a decimal.
periods_per_year
    Compounding periods per year. Defaults to 365 (daily). Must be
    greater than 0.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    APYs, as decimals.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values, or `periods_per_year` is not
    greater than 0.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import apr_to_apy
>>> # 24% APR compounded daily
>>> apr_to_apy(apr=0.24)
0.27114

months_to_payoff(balance: 'ArrayLike', monthly_payment: 'ArrayLike', apr: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Months to pay off a balance with a fixed payment.

Interest compounds monthly at `apr / 12`. The result is not rounded; the
last payment is a partial one. From the
[Managing Debt](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/managing_debt.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
balance
    Current balance. Must be greater than 0.
monthly_payment
    Fixed monthly payment. Must be greater than 0.
apr
    Annual percentage rate, as a decimal.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Months.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values, `balance` or
    `monthly_payment` is not greater than 0, or the payment does not
    cover the first month's interest (the balance would never be paid
    off).

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import months_to_payoff
>>> # $5,000 balance, $100/month, 22% APR
>>> months_to_payoff(balance=5000, monthly_payment=100, apr=0.22)
136.779

total_interest(monthly_payment: 'ArrayLike', n_months: 'ArrayLike', principal: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Total interest paid over the life of a loan.

All payments minus the amount borrowed. From the
[Managing Debt](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/managing_debt.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
monthly_payment
    Fixed monthly payment.
n_months
    Number of payments.
principal
    Amount borrowed.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Interest paid.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import total_interest
>>> # 6-year vs. 4-year car loan, $20,000 at 7%
>>> total_interest(monthly_payment=[340.98, 478.92], n_months=[72, 48],
...                principal=20000)
array([4550.56, 2988.16])

loan_income_ratio(loan_total: 'ArrayLike', expected_salary: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Total student loans as a multiple of expected starting salary.

A ratio at or below 1 means you borrow no more than your first year's
salary. From the
[Managing Debt](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/managing_debt.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
loan_total
    Total amount borrowed.
expected_salary
    Expected yearly starting salary. Must be greater than 0.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Ratios (`1.07` is 107% of salary).

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values, or `expected_salary` is not
    greater than 0.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import loan_income_ratio
>>> loan_income_ratio(loan_total=45000, expected_salary=42000)
1.0714

monthly_standard_payment(principal: 'ArrayLike', annual_rate: 'ArrayLike' = 0.065, years: 'ArrayLike' = 10) -> 'Numeric'

Monthly payment on a standard student loan repayment plan.

The same amortization formula as `mortgage_payment()`, with student loan
defaults (6.5% over 10 years). From the
[Managing Debt](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/managing_debt.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
principal
    Amount borrowed.
annual_rate
    Yearly interest rate, as a decimal. Defaults to 0.065.
years
    Repayment term in years. Defaults to 10. Must be greater than 0.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Monthly payments.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values, or `years` is not greater
    than 0.

See Also
--------
mortgage_payment : The general amortization formula.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import monthly_standard_payment
>>> monthly_standard_payment(principal=45000)
510.96

idr_monthly_payment(agi: 'ArrayLike', poverty_guideline: 'ArrayLike' = 15960, threshold_pct: 'ArrayLike' = 1.5, payment_rate: 'ArrayLike' = 0.1) -> 'Numeric'

Income driven repayment (IDR) monthly payment.

Discretionary income is adjusted gross income (AGI) above
`threshold_pct` times the poverty guideline. The yearly payment is
`payment_rate` of that, split into 12 months and rounded to cents. From
the [Managing Debt](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/managing_debt.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
agi
    Adjusted gross income.
poverty_guideline
    Federal poverty guideline for the household size. Defaults to 15960
    (one person).
threshold_pct
    Multiple of the poverty guideline that is protected. Defaults to 1.5
    (150%).
payment_rate
    Share of discretionary income paid each year. Defaults to 0.10.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Monthly payments.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import idr_monthly_payment
>>> # IBR: $50,000 AGI, 150% threshold, 10% rate
>>> idr_monthly_payment(agi=50000)
217.17
>>> # IBR for loans before July 2014: 15% rate
>>> idr_monthly_payment(agi=50000, payment_rate=0.15)
325.75

dti_ratio(monthly_debt_payments: 'ArrayLike', gross_monthly_income: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Debt to income ratio.

Monthly debt payments as a percent of gross monthly income. From the
[Managing Debt](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/managing_debt.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
monthly_debt_payments
    Total monthly debt payments.
gross_monthly_income
    Monthly income before taxes. Must be greater than 0.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Percentages (`28.3` is 28.3%).

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values, or `gross_monthly_income` is
    not greater than 0.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import dti_ratio
>>> dti_ratio(monthly_debt_payments=1061, gross_monthly_income=3750)
28.29

payoff_vs_invest(loan_rate: 'float', expected_return: 'float') -> 'str'

Pay off a debt or invest the difference.

Compares a loan's interest rate with an expected investment return. From
the [Managing Debt](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/managing_debt.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
loan_rate
    The loan's yearly interest rate, as a decimal. A single number.
expected_return
    Expected yearly investment return, as a decimal. A single number.

Returns
-------
str
    `"Pay off the debt"`, `"Invest the difference"`, or
    `"Roughly a wash; do both"`.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values or is not a single number.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import payoff_vs_invest
>>> payoff_vs_invest(loan_rate=0.05, expected_return=0.07)
'Invest the difference'

order_avalanche(debts: 'list[dict[str, Any]]') -> 'list[dict[str, Any]]'

Order debts for the avalanche method (highest APR first).

From the [Managing Debt](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/managing_debt.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
debts
    A list of dicts, each with a numeric `apr` key.

Returns
-------
list of dict
    A new list, sorted by `apr` from highest to lowest. Ties keep their
    original order.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If `debts` is not a list of dicts, or an `apr` is not numeric.
ValueError
    If a debt has no `apr` key, or an `apr` is missing.

See Also
--------
order_snowball : Smallest balance first.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import order_avalanche
>>> debts = [
...     {"name": "Card A", "balance": 1000, "apr": 0.18},
...     {"name": "Card B", "balance": 5000, "apr": 0.24},
...     {"name": "Card C", "balance": 2000, "apr": 0.15},
... ]
>>> [d["name"] for d in order_avalanche(debts)]
['Card B', 'Card A', 'Card C']

order_snowball(debts: 'list[dict[str, Any]]') -> 'list[dict[str, Any]]'

Order debts for the snowball method (smallest balance first).

From the [Managing Debt](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/managing_debt.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
debts
    A list of dicts, each with a numeric `balance` key.

Returns
-------
list of dict
    A new list, sorted by `balance` from smallest to largest. Ties keep
    their original order.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If `debts` is not a list of dicts, or a `balance` is not numeric.
ValueError
    If a debt has no `balance` key, or a `balance` is missing.

See Also
--------
order_avalanche : Highest APR first.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import order_snowball
>>> debts = [
...     {"name": "Card A", "balance": 1000, "apr": 0.18},
...     {"name": "Card B", "balance": 5000, "apr": 0.24},
...     {"name": "Card C", "balance": 2000, "apr": 0.15},
... ]
>>> [d["name"] for d in order_snowball(debts)]
['Card A', 'Card C', 'Card B']

credit_utilization(balance: 'ArrayLike', credit_limit: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Returns

    Percentages (`30` is 30%).

Raises

TypeError

    If an argument contains missing values, or `credit_limit` is not
    greater than 0.

Examples

30.0


## Emergency Fund

Foundations. Functions from the Emergency Fund chapter.


emergency_fund_target(monthly_expenses: 'ArrayLike', months: 'ArrayLike' = 3) -> 'Numeric'

Emergency fund target.

Essential monthly expenses times the number of months to cover. From the
[Emergency Fund](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/emergency_fund.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
monthly_expenses
    Essential monthly expenses.
months
    Months of expenses to cover. Defaults to 3.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Target balances.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import emergency_fund_target
>>> # 3-month and 6-month targets on $2,400/month
>>> emergency_fund_target(monthly_expenses=2400, months=[3, 6])
array([ 7200., 14400.])

months_to_ef_goal(target: 'ArrayLike', current_balance: 'ArrayLike', monthly_contribution: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Whole'

Months to reach an emergency fund target.

Rounded up to whole months. Returns 0 when the fund is already at or
above the target. From the
[Emergency Fund](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/emergency_fund.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
target
    Target balance.
current_balance
    Amount already saved.
monthly_contribution
    Amount added each month. Must be greater than 0.

Returns
-------
int or numpy.ndarray
    Whole months.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values, or `monthly_contribution` is
    not greater than 0.

See Also
--------
monthly_contribution_needed : Solve for the contribution instead.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import months_to_ef_goal
>>> months_to_ef_goal(target=9600, current_balance=1200,
...                   monthly_contribution=400)
21

monthly_contribution_needed(target: 'ArrayLike', current_balance: 'ArrayLike', months: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Whole'

Monthly contribution needed to reach an emergency fund target.

Rounded up to whole dollars. Returns 0 when the fund is already at or
above the target. From the
[Emergency Fund](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/emergency_fund.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
target
    Target balance.
current_balance
    Amount already saved.
months
    Months to reach the target. Must be greater than 0.

Returns
-------
int or numpy.ndarray
    Whole dollars per month.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values, or `months` is not greater
    than 0.

See Also
--------
months_to_ef_goal : Solve for the months instead.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import monthly_contribution_needed
>>> monthly_contribution_needed(target=9600, current_balance=1200, months=18)
467

ef_growth(balance: 'ArrayLike', apy: 'ArrayLike', months: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Emergency fund balance after earning interest.

Grows `balance` at `apy` for `months / 12` years. From the
[Emergency Fund](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/emergency_fund.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
balance
    Starting balance.
apy
    Annual percentage yield, as a decimal.
months
    Number of months.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Ending balances.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import ef_growth
>>> ef_growth(balance=9600, apy=0.04, months=12)
9984.0

## High-Yield Savings Accounts

Savings. Functions from the High-Yield Savings Accounts chapter.


hysa_balance(principal: 'ArrayLike', annual_apy: 'ArrayLike', years: 'ArrayLike' = 1) -> 'Numeric'

High-yield savings account balance.

Grows `principal` at `annual_apy` for `years`. From the
[High-Yield Savings Accounts](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/high_yield_accounts.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
principal
    Starting balance.
annual_apy
    Annual percentage yield, as a decimal.
years
    Number of years. Defaults to 1.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Ending balances.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import hysa_balance
>>> # $9,600 at 4% APY after 1 and 5 years
>>> hysa_balance(principal=9600, annual_apy=0.04, years=[1, 5])
array([ 9984.        , 11679.86786304])


## Automating Savings

Savings. Functions from the Automating Savings chapter.


monthly_savings(gross_monthly_income: 'ArrayLike', savings_rate: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Monthly amount to pay yourself first.

From the [Automating Savings](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/automating_savings.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
gross_monthly_income
    Monthly income before taxes.
savings_rate
    Share of income saved, as a decimal.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Monthly savings.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import monthly_savings
>>> monthly_savings(gross_monthly_income=4000, savings_rate=0.20)
800.0


## Investing Basics

Investing. Functions from the Investing Basics chapter.


future_value(present_value: 'ArrayLike', rate: 'ArrayLike', years: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Future value of a single amount with yearly compounding.

From the [Investing Basics](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/investing_basics.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
present_value
    Amount invested today.
rate
    Yearly return, as a decimal.
years
    Number of years.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Future values.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

See Also
--------
future_value_series : Future value of regular contributions.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import future_value
>>> # $10,000 at 7% for 10 years
>>> future_value(present_value=10000, rate=0.07, years=10)
19671.51
>>> # several horizons in one call
>>> future_value(present_value=10000, rate=0.07, years=[5, 10, 20, 30])
array([14025.517307  , 19671.5135729 , 38696.84462486, 76122.55042662])

rule_of_72(annual_return_pct: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Years for money to double, by the rule of 72.

The one function in the package that takes a percent rather than a
decimal (`7`, not `0.07`). From the
[Investing Basics](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/investing_basics.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
annual_return_pct
    Yearly return, as a percent. Must be greater than 0.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Years to double.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If `annual_return_pct` is not numeric.
ValueError
    If `annual_return_pct` contains missing values or is not greater
    than 0.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import rule_of_72
>>> rule_of_72(annual_return_pct=7)
10.28

future_value_series(contribution: 'ArrayLike', rate: 'ArrayLike', periods: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Future value of a fixed contribution made every period.

Contributions are made at the end of each period. `rate` is the rate per
period, so a monthly series uses `annual_rate / 12`. A 0% rate gives the
sum of the contributions. From the
[Investing Basics](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/investing_basics.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
contribution
    Amount contributed each period.
rate
    Return per period, as a decimal.
periods
    Number of periods.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Future values.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

See Also
--------
future_value : Future value of a single amount.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import future_value_series
>>> # $500/month for 30 years at 7% a year
>>> future_value_series(contribution=500, rate=0.07 / 12, periods=30 * 12)
609985.49

real_return(nominal: 'ArrayLike', inflation: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Real (inflation adjusted) return.

From the [Investing Basics](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/investing_basics.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
nominal
    Nominal yearly return, as a decimal.
inflation
    Yearly inflation rate, as a decimal.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Real returns, as decimals.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import real_return
>>> real_return(nominal=0.07, inflation=0.03)
0.03883


## Retirement Accounts

Investing. Functions from the Retirement Accounts chapter.


employer_match(salary: 'ArrayLike', contribution_pct: 'ArrayLike', match_limit_pct: 'ArrayLike', match_rate: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Yearly employer match on retirement contributions.

The employer matches `match_rate` of your contributions, up to
`match_limit_pct` of salary. From the
[Retirement Accounts](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/retirement_accounts.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
salary
    Yearly salary.
contribution_pct
    Share of salary you contribute, as a decimal.
match_limit_pct
    Share of salary the employer matches up to, as a decimal.
match_rate
    Share of each matched dollar the employer adds, as a decimal.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Yearly employer contributions.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import employer_match
>>> # $45,000 salary, 50% match on the first 6%, contributing 6% or 3%
>>> employer_match(salary=45000, contribution_pct=[0.06, 0.03],
...                match_limit_pct=0.06, match_rate=0.50)
array([1350.,  675.])

after_tax_value(contribution: 'ArrayLike', tax_rate: 'ArrayLike', rate: 'ArrayLike', years: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

After tax value of a retirement contribution.

Taxes the contribution once at `tax_rate`, then grows it. With the same
rate and return, it doesn't matter whether the tax comes first (Roth) or
last (Traditional); only the tax rate does. From the
[Retirement Accounts](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/retirement_accounts.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
contribution
    Amount contributed.
tax_rate
    Tax rate applied, as a decimal.
rate
    Yearly return, as a decimal.
years
    Number of years.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    After tax values.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import after_tax_value
>>> # Roth at 12% today vs. Traditional at 22% in retirement
>>> after_tax_value(contribution=1000, tax_rate=[0.12, 0.22], rate=0.07,
...                 years=40)
array([13177.5228985 , 11680.07711458])

future_value_after_fees(contribution: 'ArrayLike', annual_return: 'ArrayLike', expense_ratio: 'ArrayLike', years: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Future value of monthly contributions after fund fees.

Subtracts the expense ratio from the yearly return, then compounds
monthly contributions. From the
[Index Funds](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/index_funds.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
contribution
    Amount contributed each month.
annual_return

expense_ratio
    Yearly expense ratio, as a decimal.
years
    Number of years.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Future values.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import future_value_after_fees
>>> # $300/month for 40 years at 7%, index fund vs. active fund
>>> future_value_after_fees(300, 0.07, [0.0004, 0.01], 40)
array([778654.71, 597447.22])


## Asset Allocation

Investing. Functions from the Asset Allocation chapter.


portfolio_return(stock_pct: 'ArrayLike | pl.Expr', stock_return: 'ArrayLike | pl.Expr', bond_return: 'ArrayLike | pl.Expr') -> 'Any'

Return on a two fund (stock and bond) portfolio.

A weighted average of the two returns. Also accepts polars expressions,
so it works inside `with_columns()`. From the
[Asset Allocation](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/asset_allocation.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
stock_pct
    Share of the portfolio in stocks, as a decimal.
stock_return
    Yearly stock return, as a decimal.
bond_return
    Yearly bond return, as a decimal.

Returns
-------
float, numpy.ndarray, or polars.Expr
    Portfolio returns, as decimals. A polars expression when any input is
    one.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric (or a polars expression).
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> import polars as pl
>>> from perfinpy import portfolio_return
>>> # an 80/20 portfolio in an average year
>>> portfolio_return(stock_pct=0.80, stock_return=0.10, bond_return=0.04)
0.088
>>> # 100/0, 80/20, and 60/40 in a bad year
>>> pl.DataFrame({"stocks": [1.0, 0.8, 0.6]}).with_columns(
...     bad=portfolio_return(pl.col("stocks"), -0.40, 0.0)
... )["bad"].round(2).to_list()
[-0.4, -0.32, -0.24]

rebalance_amount(target_pct: 'ArrayLike', total: 'ArrayLike', current_amount: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Amount to buy (positive) or sell (negative) to reach a target.

From the [Asset Allocation](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/asset_allocation.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
target_pct
    Target share of the portfolio, as a decimal.
total
    Total portfolio value.
current_amount
    Current value of the holding.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Amounts to buy (positive) or sell (negative).

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import rebalance_amount
>>> # $5,600 in stocks and $2,000 in bonds after a 30% stock drop
>>> rebalance_amount(target_pct=0.80, total=5600 + 2000, current_amount=5600)
480.0


## Taxes

Taxes and insurance. Functions from the Taxes chapter.


income_tax(income: 'float', deduction: 'float' = 16100) -> 'float'

Federal income tax for a single filer (2026 brackets).

Subtracts the deduction, then taxes each slice of taxable income at its
bracket's rate. Uses the 2026 single filer brackets and standard
deduction. From the
[Taxes](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/taxes.html) chapter.

Parameters
----------
income
    Yearly gross income. A single number.
deduction
    Deduction subtracted before tax. Defaults to 16100 (the 2026
    standard deduction). A single number.

Returns
-------
float
    Tax owed.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values or is not a single number.

See Also
--------
raise_kept : How much of a raise you keep after tax.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import income_tax
>>> income_tax(income=45000)
3220.0
>>> # effective rate
>>> income_tax(income=45000) / 45000
0.0715

raise_kept(old_income: 'float', raise_amount: 'float') -> 'float'

How much of a raise you keep after federal income tax.

The raise minus the extra tax it adds, using `income_tax()`. From the
[Taxes](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/taxes.html) chapter.

Parameters
----------
old_income
    Yearly gross income before the raise. A single number.
raise_amount
    Size of the raise. A single number.

Returns
-------
float
    Amount of the raise kept after tax.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values or is not a single number.

See Also
--------
income_tax : The tax calculation used here.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import raise_kept
>>> # $2,000 raise on a $66,000 salary
>>> raise_kept(old_income=66000, raise_amount=2000)
1610.0


## Insurance

Taxes and insurance. Functions from the Insurance chapter.


break_even_years(high_deductible: 'ArrayLike', low_deductible: 'ArrayLike', yearly_savings: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Years of premium savings to cover a higher deductible.

If you go longer than this between claims, the higher deductible comes
out ahead. From the
[Insurance](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/insurance.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
high_deductible
    The higher deductible.
low_deductible
    The lower deductible.
yearly_savings
    Yearly premium saved by choosing the higher deductible. Must be
    greater than 0.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Years.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values, or `yearly_savings` is not
    greater than 0.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import break_even_years
>>> break_even_years(high_deductible=1000, low_deductible=500,
...                  yearly_savings=150)
3.33

plan_cost(monthly_premium: 'ArrayLike', medical_cost: 'ArrayLike', oop_max: 'ArrayLike', employer_hsa: 'ArrayLike' = 0) -> 'Numeric'

Yearly cost of a health plan.

Twelve premiums plus what you pay for care (capped at the out of pocket
maximum), minus any employer HSA contribution. Use `float("inf")` for
`medical_cost` to get the worst case year. From the
[Insurance](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/insurance.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
monthly_premium
    Monthly premium.
medical_cost
    Medical costs for the year.
oop_max
    Out of pocket maximum.
employer_hsa
    Employer HSA contribution. Defaults to 0.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Yearly costs.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import plan_cost
>>> # Plan A in a healthy year ($300 of care) and the worst year
>>> plan_cost(100, [300, float("inf")], oop_max=3000)
array([1500., 4200.])
>>> # Plan B, with a $500 employer HSA contribution
>>> plan_cost(40, [300, float("inf")], oop_max=5000, employer_hsa=500)
array([ 280., 4980.])


## Financial Goals

Planning. Functions from the Financial Goals chapter.


monthly_for_goal(goal: 'ArrayLike', annual_rate: 'ArrayLike', months: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Monthly saving needed to reach a goal.

Solves the future value of a series for the contribution, compounding
monthly at `annual_rate / 12`. A 0% rate gives `goal / months`. From the
[Financial Goals](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/financial_goals.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
goal
    Amount needed.
annual_rate
    Yearly return on savings, as a decimal.
months
    Months until the goal. Must be greater than 0.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Monthly contributions.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values, or `months` is not greater
    than 0.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import monthly_for_goal
>>> # $15,000 in 5 years at 4%, compared to no interest
>>> monthly_for_goal(goal=15000, annual_rate=[0.04, 0], months=60)
array([226.24783083, 250.        ])

months_to_fund(goal: 'ArrayLike', monthly: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Whole'

Whole months to fund a goal with no interest.

From the [Financial Goals](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/financial_goals.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
goal
    Amount needed.
monthly
    Amount saved each month. Must be greater than 0.

Returns
-------
int or numpy.ndarray
    Whole months, rounded up.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values, or `monthly` is not greater
    than 0.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import months_to_fund
>>> # one at a time: a $3,000 trip, then a $9,000 car, at $600/month
>>> months_to_fund(3000, 600), months_to_fund(3000 + 9000, 600)
(5, 20)


## Major Purchases

Planning. Functions from the Major Purchases chapter.


rent_buy_threshold(home_value: 'ArrayLike', unrecoverable_rate: 'ArrayLike' = 0.05) -> 'Numeric'

Monthly rent that matches the unrecoverable cost of owning.

The 5% rule: property tax, maintenance, and the cost of capital come to
about 5% of the home's value each year. Rent below this monthly amount
favors renting. From the
[Major Purchases](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/major_purchases.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
home_value
    Price of the home.
unrecoverable_rate
    Yearly unrecoverable cost, as a decimal. Defaults to 0.05.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Monthly rent thresholds.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import rent_buy_threshold
>>> rent_buy_threshold(home_value=500000)
2083.33

mortgage_payment(principal: 'ArrayLike', annual_rate: 'ArrayLike', years: 'ArrayLike') -> 'Numeric'

Monthly payment on a fixed rate loan.

The standard amortization formula with monthly compounding. A 0% rate
gives `principal / (years * 12)`. From the
[Major Purchases](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/major_purchases.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
principal
    Amount borrowed.
annual_rate
    Yearly interest rate, as a decimal.
years
    Loan term in years. Must be greater than 0.

Returns
-------
float or numpy.ndarray
    Monthly payments (principal and interest only).

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values, or `years` is not greater
    than 0.

See Also
--------
first_payment_split : Interest and principal in the first payment.
monthly_standard_payment : Student loan defaults.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import mortgage_payment
>>> # $480,000 loan at 6% over 30 years
>>> mortgage_payment(principal=480000, annual_rate=0.06, years=30)
2877.84

first_payment_split(principal: 'float', annual_rate: 'float', years: 'float') -> 'dict[str, float]'

Interest and principal in a loan's first monthly payment.

From the [Major Purchases](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/major_purchases.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
principal
    Amount borrowed. A single number.
annual_rate
    Yearly interest rate, as a decimal. A single number.
years
    Loan term in years. A single number greater than 0.

Returns
-------
dict
    Keys `payment`, `interest`, `principal`, and `pct_interest` (the
    share of the payment that is interest, as a percent).

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an argument is not numeric.
ValueError
    If an argument contains missing values or is not a single number, or
    `years` is not greater than 0.

See Also
--------
mortgage_payment : The payment formula used here.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import first_payment_split
>>> split = first_payment_split(principal=480000, annual_rate=0.06, years=30)
>>> {k: round(v, 2) for k, v in split.items()}
{'payment': 2877.84, 'interest': 2400.0, 'principal': 477.84, 'pct_interest': 83.4}


## Estate Planning

Planning. Functions from the Estate Planning chapter.


net_worth(assets: 'Mapping[str, float] | ArrayLike', debts: 'Mapping[str, float] | ArrayLike') -> 'float'

Net worth: total assets minus total debts.

From the [Estate Planning](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/estate_planning.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
assets
    Asset values, as a dict of name to amount or a sequence of amounts.
debts
    Debt balances, as a dict of name to amount or a sequence of amounts.

Returns
-------
float
    Net worth.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If a value is not numeric.
ValueError
    If a value is missing.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import net_worth
>>> assets = {"401k": 12000, "roth_ira": 6000, "savings": 8000, "car": 9000}
>>> debts = {"car_loan": 6000, "credit_card": 1000}
>>> net_worth(assets, debts)
28000.0

beneficiary_share(with_beneficiary: 'Mapping[str, float] | ArrayLike', without_beneficiary: 'Mapping[str, float] | ArrayLike') -> 'float'

Share of assets that pass directly to a named beneficiary.

Assets with a beneficiary (retirement accounts, life insurance, payable
on death accounts) skip probate. From the
[Estate Planning](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/estate_planning.html)
chapter.

Parameters
----------
with_beneficiary
    Values of assets with a named beneficiary, as a dict or a sequence.
without_beneficiary
    Values of assets without one, as a dict or a sequence.

Returns
-------
float
    Share, as a decimal (`0.8875` is 88.75%).

Raises
------
TypeError
    If a value is not numeric.
ValueError
    If a value is missing, or total assets are not greater than 0.

Examples
--------
>>> from perfinpy import beneficiary_share
>>> with_beneficiary = {"401k": 12000, "roth_ira": 6000,
...                     "life_insurance": 45000, "savings_pod": 8000}
>>> beneficiary_share(with_beneficiary, {"car": 9000})
0.8875


----------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the User Guide documentation for the package.
----------------------------------------------------------------------


## Get started

### Get started

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import polars as pl
from perfinpy import *
```

`perfinpy` holds the Python functions from [Personal Finance: a field manual](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/). Each chapter of the book builds its calculations from scratch so you can see how the formula works. This package collects those same functions, documents them, and tests them, so you can use them without copying code out of the book. On this page I'll cover how to install `perfinpy` and the conventions every function follows. Then we'll take a short tour with one example from each part of the book.

## Installation

`perfinpy` isn't on PyPI. Install the development version from GitHub:

```bash
uv pip install git+https://github.com/mjfrigaard/perfinpy
```

`perfinpy` depends on `numpy` and `polars`. If you work in R, the same functions are in [perfinr](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/perfinr/).

## Conventions

The functions keep the names, arguments, and defaults from the book, so code from a chapter runs unchanged after `from perfinpy import *`. A few rules hold across the whole package:

| Rule | Example |
|---|---|
| Rates and returns are decimals | `0.07` is 7% |
| The one exception is `rule_of_72()`, which takes a percent | `rule_of_72(7)` |
| Ratio functions return percents | `percent_of_income(1500, 5000)` returns `30.0`, not `0.30` |
| Two ratios stay decimals, as in the book | `loan_income_ratio()` (`1.07`) and `beneficiary_share()` (`0.8875`) |
| Most functions accept arrays | `future_value(10000, 0.07, [10, 20])` returns a `numpy` array |
| Single numbers in, a `float` out | `future_value(10000, 0.07, 10)` returns a `float` |
| A few functions take single values only | `income_tax()`, `raise_kept()`, `payoff_vs_invest()`, `first_payment_split()` |
| A 0% rate returns the no interest answer | `mortgage_payment(120000, 0, 30)` is `120000 / 360` |
| Bad inputs raise an error | text raises `TypeError`; `nan`, or a zero where a divisor is needed, raises `ValueError` |

Array inputs make it easy to compare options side by side. Here is the same \$10,000 at 7% over four horizons:

```{python}
#| label: vectorized
years = [5, 10, 20, 30]
pl.DataFrame({
    "years": years,
    "value": future_value(present_value=10000, rate=0.07, years=years),
})
```

When an input doesn't make sense, the function says which argument is wrong instead of returning `inf` or `nan`:

```{python}
#| label: error
#| error: true
percent_of_income(expense=1500, income=0)
```

## How the user guide maps to the book

There is one page for each chapter of the book. Each one takes the chapter's examples (with the same numbers), shows the bar model, and then answers the question with perfinpy functions.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 7
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "darkMode":false}}}%%
flowchart TD
    Book(["Personal Finance: a field manual"])

    subgraph Foundations["<strong>Foundations</strong>"]
        F1("Income")
        F2("Tracking Spending")
        F3("Budgeting")
        F4("Managing Debt")
        F5("Emergency Fund")
    end

    subgraph Savings["<strong>Savings</strong>"]
        S1("Savings Strategies")
        S2("High-Yield Savings Accounts")
        S3("Automating Savings")
    end

    subgraph Investing["<strong>Investing</strong>"]
        I1("Investing Basics")
        I2("Retirement Accounts")
        I3("Index Funds")
        I4("Asset Allocation")
    end

    subgraph TaxIns["<strong>Taxes and insurance</strong>"]
        T1("Taxes")
        T2("Insurance")
    end

    subgraph Planning["<strong>Planning</strong>"]
        P1("Financial Goals")

    end
```

## A short tour

Each example below uses the numbers from the book, so you can check the result against the chapter.

### Foundations

Rent of \$1,500 on a \$5,000 monthly income:

```{python}
#| label: tour-foundations
rent_share = percent_of_income(expense=1500, income=5000)
rent_share
```

Rent takes `{python} f"{rent_share:.0f}"`% of income. A \$5,000 credit card balance at 22% APR, paying \$100 a month:

```{python}
#| label: tour-debt
payoff = months_to_payoff(balance=5000, monthly_payment=100, apr=0.22)
payoff
```

That is about `{python} f"{payoff / 12:.1f}"` years of payments.

### Savings

Spending \$2,720 of a \$3,200 take home paycheck:

```{python}
#| label: tour-savings
savings_rate(income=3200, spending=2720)
```

### Investing

\$10,000 invested at 7% for 10 years:

```{python}
#| label: tour-investing
future_value(present_value=10000, rate=0.07, years=10)
```

### Taxes and insurance

2026 federal income tax on a \$45,000 salary (single filer), and the effective rate:

```{python}
#| label: tour-taxes
tax = income_tax(income=45000)
tax, tax / 45000
```

The effective rate is `{python} f"{tax / 45000 * 100:.1f}"`%, well below the 12% top bracket this salary reaches.

### Planning

The monthly payment on a \$480,000 mortgage at 6% over 30 years:

```{python}
#| label: tour-planning
mortgage_payment(principal=480000, annual_rate=0.06, years=30)
```

## Foundations

### Income

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import polars as pl
from perfinpy import *
```

A bigger paycheck only builds wealth if some of it stays put. The book's [Income](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/income.html) chapter turns that idea into three questions. How much does steady saving grow into? How much of each paycheck is committed before you spend a dollar? And what is a raise worth if you invest part of it? In this page I'll answer each one with `perfinpy`, using the same numbers as the chapter.

| Function | Returns | Units |
|---|---|---|
| `wealth_formula()` | the balance after saving part of a yearly income every year | dollars; rates go in as decimals |
| `fixed_cost_ratio()` | monthly fixed costs as a share of take home pay | percent (`55`, not `0.55`) |
| `raise_invested_value()` | the balance after investing part of a monthly raise every month | dollars; rates go in as decimals |

The units follow the package conventions described in [Get started](00-get-started.qmd): rates go in as decimals and ratios come out as percents.

## How much does steady saving grow into?

The chapter builds on Scott Galloway's wealth formula (focus plus stoicism, time, and diversification multiplied together). To put numbers on it, the book uses a worker who earns about the 2025 median for full time workers. This worker saves a fixed share of income every year and invests it. The scenario below sets those inputs:

```{python}
#| label: wealth-scenario
income = 62400
save_pct = 0.15
annual_return = 0.08
wealth_years = 40
```

This worker earns \$`{python} f"{income:,}"` a year and saves `{python} f"{save_pct * 100:.0f}"`% of it, which comes to \$`{python} f"{income * save_pct:,.0f}"` a year. Those savings earn `{python} f"{annual_return * 100:.0f}"`% a year for `{python} wealth_years` years. Each bar below is the balance at a checkpoint, split into the money put in and what it grew into.

![Money put in vs. growth at each checkpoint](assets/income-wealth-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Stacked bar chart of savings at years 10, 20, 30, and 40 from depositing $9,360 a year at 8%. Each bar splits into money put in (green, bottom) and growth (blue, top). The bar totals are $136k, $428k, $1,060k, and $2,425k. Growth is the smaller layer at year 10 and fills most of the bar by year 40."}

The green layer rises in a straight line because it is one deposit per year. The blue layer is every deposit growing for the years it has left, and it is the part that takes over. `wealth_formula()` adds up all of those growing deposits in one call:

```{python}
#| label: wealth-40
wealth_40 = wealth_formula(
    median_income=income,
    savings_rate=save_pct,
    annual_return=annual_return,
    years=wealth_years,
)
wealth_40
```

After `{python} wealth_years` years the balance is about \$`{python} f"{wealth_40:,.0f}"`. Only \$`{python} f"{income * save_pct * wealth_years:,.0f}"` of that is money the worker put in; the other \$`{python} f"{wealth_40 - income * save_pct * wealth_years:,.0f}"` is growth.

## How much of your paycheck is already spoken for?

Fixed costs (rent, loan payments, insurance, utilities) are the bills you can't easily change from one month to the next. The book's example is a first job with these monthly numbers:

```{python}
#| label: fixed-scenario
fixed_costs = 1760
take_home = 3200
ceiling_pct = 60
```

This paycheck brings in \$`{python} f"{take_home:,}"` of take home pay a month, and \$`{python} f"{fixed_costs:,}"` of it goes to fixed costs. The book suggests keeping fixed costs under `{python} ceiling_pct`% of take home pay, which is \$`{python} f"{take_home * ceiling_pct / 100:,.0f}"` here. The bar below cuts the paycheck into ten equal pieces and marks that ceiling.

![Take home pay split into fixed costs and flexible spending](assets/income-fixed-cost-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Bar model: one horizontal bar for $3,200 of take home pay, divided by white lines into ten $320 pieces. Fixed costs of $1,760 (vermillion) fill five and a half pieces, and flexible spending of $1,440 (light green) fills the rest. A dashed line marks the 60% ceiling at $1,920, just to the right of where fixed costs end."}

`fixed_cost_ratio()` divides the fixed costs by take home pay and returns a percent:

```{python}
#| label: fixed-ratio
ratio = fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs=fixed_costs, take_home=take_home)
ratio
```

Fixed costs take `{python} f"{ratio:g}"`% of this paycheck, under the `{python} ceiling_pct`% ceiling. That leaves \$`{python} f"{take_home * ceiling_pct / 100 - fixed_costs:,.0f}"` of room before a new commitment pushes the budget past it. The [Budgeting](03-budgeting.qmd) page picks up from here and splits the flexible part of the paycheck.

## What is a raise really worth?

The chapter recommends splitting every raise: half goes to your lifestyle and half gets invested. The book's raise adds a fixed amount to monthly take home pay:

```{python}
#| label: raise-scenario
monthly_raise = 400
share = 0.5
raise_rate = 0.07
raise_years = 25
```

A raise of \$`{python} f"{monthly_raise:,}"` a month split in half sends \$`{python} f"{monthly_raise * share:,.0f}"` a month into investments. That money earns `{python} f"{raise_rate * 100:.0f}"`% a year for `{python} raise_years` years. The bars below show the balance at each checkpoint.

![A monthly raise contribution invested at each checkpoint](assets/income-raise-value-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Stacked bar chart of $200 a month invested at a 7% annual return, at years 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25. Each bar splits into money put in (green, bottom) and growth (blue, top). The bar totals are $14k, $35k, $63k, $104k, and $162k. By year 25 the growth layer is larger than the money put in."}

`raise_invested_value()` takes the whole raise and the share you invest, then compounds the contributions monthly:

```{python}
#| label: raise-value
raise_value = raise_invested_value(
    monthly_raise=monthly_raise,
    invest_share=share,
    rate=raise_rate,
    years=raise_years,
)
raise_value
```

Half of the raise grows to about \$`{python} f"{raise_value:,.0f}"`. The contributions add up to \$`{python} f"{monthly_raise * share * 12 * raise_years:,.0f}"`, so growth adds about \$`{python} f"{raise_value - monthly_raise * share * 12 * raise_years:,.0f}"`. The [Investing Basics](09-investing-basics.qmd) page returns to this future value of contributions formula with `future_value_series()`.

## Variations

Both growth functions accept arrays, so we can compare options in one call. The savings rate is the stoicism lever in Galloway's formula. The code below keeps the income, return, and horizon from the first section and changes only the share saved:

```{python}
#| label: variations-savings-rate
rates = [0.10, 0.15, 0.20]
pl.DataFrame({
    "savings_rate": rates,
    "yearly_savings": [income * r for r in rates],
    "wealth": wealth_formula(
        median_income=income,
        savings_rate=rates,
        annual_return=annual_return,
        years=wealth_years,
    ),
})
```

The same idea works for the raise. Here is the \$`{python} f"{monthly_raise:,}"` raise with a quarter, half, three quarters, and all of it invested:

```{python}
#| label: variations-raise-share
shares = [0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0]
pl.DataFrame({
    "invest_share": shares,
    "per_month": [monthly_raise * s for s in shares],
    "value": raise_invested_value(
        monthly_raise=monthly_raise,
        invest_share=shares,
        rate=raise_rate,
        years=raise_years,
    ),
})
```

Both tables scale in a straight line with the share saved because the return and horizon don't change. The horizon is where the curve bends, as the bar models above show.

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
* `wealth_formula()` assumes one deposit at the end of every year, the same income every year (no raises), and the same return every year. It ignores taxes, fees, and inflation, so results are in future dollars.
* `raise_invested_value()` makes the same assumptions with a deposit at the end of every month and monthly compounding.
* A 0% return in either function gives the plain sum of the deposits instead of `nan`.
* `fixed_cost_ratio()` raises a `ValueError` when `take_home` is 0 or negative. It doesn't decide which bills count as fixed, and the 60% ceiling is a guideline from the book, not an argument.
* The growth functions reject text and `nan` but not negative values, so check the signs of your inputs.
:::

## Putting it together

The worker from the fixed cost section gets the \$`{python} f"{monthly_raise:,}"` raise. Investing half is the easy part; the real question is where the lifestyle half goes. If it stays flexible (dinners, trips), fixed costs don't change. If it goes to a pricier apartment, fixed costs rise by the full lifestyle half. The code below compares the fixed cost ratio before the raise and under both choices:

```{python}
#| label: together-ratio
new_take_home = take_home + monthly_raise
plans = pl.DataFrame({
    "plan": [
        "before the raise",
        "lifestyle half stays flexible",
        "lifestyle half goes to rent",
    ],
    "fixed_costs": [
        float(fixed_costs),
        float(fixed_costs),
        fixed_costs + monthly_raise * (1 - share),
    ],
    "take_home": [take_home, new_take_home, new_take_home],
})
plans = plans.with_columns(
    ratio=fixed_cost_ratio(
        fixed_costs=plans["fixed_costs"].to_numpy(),
        take_home=plans["take_home"].to_numpy(),
    )
)
plans
```

Keeping the lifestyle half flexible drops the ratio to `{python} f"{plans['ratio'][1]:.1f}"`%. Moving it into rent leaves the ratio at `{python} f"{plans['ratio'][2]:.1f}"`%, almost where it started, so the raise buys very little breathing room. This is the lifestyle inflation the chapter warns about: the upgrade becomes a permanent bill.

The invested half grows the same way in both plans. The code below values it twice: once with monthly deposits, and once with a single deposit at the end of each year. The yearly version uses `wealth_formula()`, whose `median_income` argument accepts any yearly amount:

```{python}
#| label: together-invest
monthly_value = raise_invested_value(
    monthly_raise=monthly_raise,
    invest_share=share,
    rate=raise_rate,
    years=raise_years,
)
yearly_value = wealth_formula(
    median_income=monthly_raise * 12,
    savings_rate=share,
    annual_return=raise_rate,
    years=raise_years,
)
monthly_value, yearly_value
```

The same dollars come out about \$`{python} f"{monthly_value - yearly_value:,.0f}"` ahead when they're invested every month. Each monthly deposit starts growing sooner, which is one more reason to automate the transfer the day the raise arrives.

## Recap

`wealth_formula()` and `raise_invested_value()` show how a steady deposit turns into a balance that is mostly growth. Time does more of the work than the deposits do. `fixed_cost_ratio()` tells you how much of each paycheck is committed before you spend anything, and returns a percent you can compare against the `{python} ceiling_pct`% ceiling. Together they make the chapter's advice measurable: keep fixed costs low, and invest part of every raise before your lifestyle absorbs it.

* [Income](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/income.html) in Personal Finance: a field manual
* Reference: `wealth_formula()`, `fixed_cost_ratio()`, `raise_invested_value()`
* Next: [Tracking Spending](02-tracking-spending.qmd)


### Tracking Spending

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import polars as pl
from perfinpy import *
```

A bank export tells you every dollar that left your account, but it doesn't tell you where your money went. To answer that, each transaction needs a category, and the small recurring charges need a second look. The [Tracking Spending](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/tracking_spending.html) chapter of the book covers both questions. In this page I'll answer them with two perfinpy functions. `apply_rules()` sorts transactions into buckets. `subscription_opportunity_cost()` shows what a subscription would have grown to if you had invested the money instead.

| Function | Returns | Units |
|---|---|---|
| `apply_rules()` | the transactions with a `Category` column added | text categories; `"Other"` when nothing matches |
| `subscription_opportunity_cost()` | what the yearly cost grows to if invested | dollars; `rate` is a decimal (`0.07` is 7%) |

## Where did the money go?

The book starts with a January 2026 bank export. It has the three columns most banks include: `Date`, `Description`, and `Amount` (negative for money going out, positive for money coming in). The code below builds the same statement as a `polars` DataFrame:

```{python}
#| label: bank-statement
bank_statement = pl.DataFrame({
    "Date": [
        "2026-01-02", "2026-01-02", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-03",
        "2026-01-04", "2026-01-04", "2026-01-05", "2026-01-06",
        "2026-01-07", "2026-01-08", "2026-01-09", "2026-01-10",
        "2026-01-11", "2026-01-12", "2026-01-13", "2026-01-14",
        "2026-01-15",
    ],
    "Description": [
        "Employer Payroll",     "Rent",
        "Comcast Internet",     "Trader Joe's",
        "Shell Gas",            "Netflix",
        "Starbucks",            "PG&E Electric",
        "AT&T Wireless",        "Spotify",
        "Whole Foods",          "Chipotle",
        "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital",
        "Shell Gas",            "Costco",
        "24 Hour Fitness",
    ],
    "Amount": [
         2400.00, -1500.00,
          -75.00,   -82.45,
          -45.20,   -15.99,
           -6.75,  -142.30,
          -85.00,   -10.99,
          -64.12,   -14.50,
         -125.00,   -17.00,
          -42.80,  -156.78,
          -39.99,
    ],
}).with_columns(pl.col("Date").str.to_date())
```

The statement has `{python} bank_statement.height` transactions and no `Category` column. To add one, we map each description to a bucket with a lookup table of keyword patterns. Each `Pattern` is a regular expression (a text search pattern), so `|` means "or" and one rule can cover several merchants:

```{python}
#| label: rules
rules = pl.DataFrame({
    "Pattern": ["Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast|PG&E|AT&T",
                "Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco", "Shell",
                "Starbucks|Chipotle",
                "Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", "Geico"],
    "Category": ["Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Groceries",
                 "Transportation", "Dining", "Subscriptions", "Insurance"],
})
```

`apply_rules()` checks the `{python} rules.height` rules in order against each description and keeps the first match. The table below shows each transaction next to the bucket it landed in:

```{python}
#| label: categorize
categorized = apply_rules(df=bank_statement, rules=rules)
categorized.select("Description", "Amount", "Category")
```

Every transaction found a bucket, so nothing fell through to `"Other"`. With a `Category` column in place, the tracking questions from the book become one line of `polars`. The code below totals each category:

```{python}
#| label: category-totals
totals = categorized.group_by("Category").agg(pl.col("Amount").sum()).sort("Category")
totals
```

```{python}
#| label: subs-total
#| include: false
subs_total = -totals.filter(pl.col("Category") == "Subscriptions")["Amount"][0]
```

Subscriptions took \$`{python} f"{subs_total:,.2f}"` in the first half of January. That total is small next to rent, but it repeats every month, which is why the next section looks at it more closely.

### When a transaction doesn't match

New merchants show up every month. The book's rule is "when in doubt, Other." A transaction that matches no pattern lands in `"Other"` until you've seen it often enough to deserve its own rule. The code below runs two new transactions through the same rules:

```{python}
#| label: unmatched
new_transactions = pl.DataFrame({
    "Description": ["Venmo Payment", "SPOTIFY FAMILY PLAN"],
})
apply_rules(df=new_transactions, rules=rules)
```

The Venmo payment falls through to `"Other"`. The Spotify charge still lands in `"Subscriptions"` because `apply_rules()` ignores case, so `"Spotify"` matches `"SPOTIFY"`.

## What does a subscription really cost?

A subscription's real cost is its opportunity cost: the money you give up by spending instead of investing. The book's example is a monthly subscription you don't really use, with the money invested instead at a real return (the return after inflation). The code below stores the book's inputs:

```{python}
#| label: subscription-inputs
monthly_cost = 20
years = 30
rate = 0.07
```

Canceling the \$`{python} monthly_cost` a month subscription frees up \$`{python} f"{monthly_cost * 12:,}"` a year to invest at `{python} f"{rate * 100:.0f}"`% for `{python} years` years. The chart below shows what that money grows into at each checkpoint, split into the money you put in and the growth it earned.

![\$240 a year invested at 7% instead of a \$20/month subscription](assets/tracking-spending-subscription-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Stacked bar chart of $240 a year invested at 7%, with bars at years 1, 5, 10, 20, and 30. Each bar splits into money put in (bluish green, bottom) and growth (vermillion, top). The totals are $240, $1,380, $3,316, $9,839, and $22,671. Growth is a thin sliver at year 5, about equal to the money put in at year 20, and roughly twice the money put in at year 30."}

Each bar adds another year's deposit to everything saved so far, and the whole pile grows by 7%. `subscription_opportunity_cost()` adds up every year's deposit and its growth in one step:

```{python}
#| label: subscription-cost
sub_cost = subscription_opportunity_cost(
    monthly_cost=monthly_cost,
    years=years,
    rate=rate,
)
sub_cost
```

Over `{python} years` years you put in \$`{python} f"{monthly_cost * 12 * years:,}"`, and growth adds \$`{python} f"{sub_cost - monthly_cost * 12 * years:,.0f}"` on top of it. That "small" \$`{python} monthly_cost` a month is a \$`{python} f"{sub_cost:,.0f}"` decision.

## Comparing horizons

`subscription_opportunity_cost()` accepts arrays, so one call can fill in every bar of the chart above. The code below puts the five checkpoints in a `pl.DataFrame` with the money put in and the growth:

```{python}
#| label: subscription-years
checkpoints = [1, 5, 10, 20, 30]
horizons = pl.DataFrame({
    "years": checkpoints,
    "put_in": [monthly_cost * 12 * y for y in checkpoints],
    "value": subscription_opportunity_cost(monthly_cost, checkpoints, rate).round(2),
}).with_columns(growth=pl.col("value") - pl.col("put_in"))
horizons
```

Growth is \$`{python} f"{horizons['growth'][1]:,.0f}"` after `{python} checkpoints[1]` years and \$`{python} f"{horizons['growth'][4]:,.0f}"` after `{python} checkpoints[4]`. Most of the cost of a subscription shows up late, which is exactly when you've stopped noticing the charge.

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
* `apply_rules()`: the first matching rule wins, so put specific patterns above general ones. Patterns are regular expressions with case ignored, so characters like `.`, `+`, and `(` have special meanings. The function only reads `Description`; a Netflix refund lands in `"Subscriptions"` just like the charge. An existing `Category` column is replaced. Both arguments must be `polars` DataFrames.
* `subscription_opportunity_cost()`: it invests the yearly total once, at the end of each year, at one fixed rate. The book's \$267,000 figure for \$219 a month assumes monthly deposits, so it comes out higher than this function's result for the same inputs. The 7% default is a real return, so the result is in today's dollars. It does not reject negative costs.
:::

## Putting it together

The book's monthly review ends with a subscription audit: list every recurring charge and decide whether it's worth the cost. The categorized statement already holds that list. The code below pulls the subscription rows and prices each one over the same horizon:

```{python}
#| label: subscription-audit
subs = categorized.filter(pl.col("Category") == "Subscriptions")
monthly = -subs["Amount"]
audit = pl.DataFrame({
    "Description": subs["Description"],
    "monthly": monthly,
    "cost_30": subscription_opportunity_cost(monthly.to_numpy(), years=years).round(2),
})
audit
```

These `{python} audit.height` subscriptions cost \$`{python} f"{audit['monthly'].sum():,.2f}"` a month, which adds up to \$`{python} f"{audit['cost_30'].sum():,.0f}"` over `{python} years` years. To put the monthly total in context, `percent_of_income()` from the [Budgeting](03-budgeting.qmd) page compares it with the paycheck on the statement:

```{python}
#| label: subscription-share
paycheck = categorized.filter(pl.col("Category") == "Income")["Amount"][0]
subs_share = percent_of_income(expense=audit["monthly"].sum(), income=paycheck)
subs_share
```

```{python}
#| label: gym-cost
#| include: false
gym_cost = audit.filter(pl.col("Description") == "24 Hour Fitness")["cost_30"][0]
```

Subscriptions take about `{python} f"{subs_share:.1f}"`% of the paycheck. As in the rest of perfinpy, the ratio comes out as a percent, not a decimal (see the conventions in [Get started](00-get-started.qmd)). The gym membership alone accounts for \$`{python} f"{gym_cost:,.0f}"` of the `{python} years` year total. That makes it the first one to check against the book's audit question: have you used it in the last 30 days?

## Recap

`apply_rules()` turns a bank export into categorized spending with a small, stable table of keyword patterns, and anything new falls through to `"Other"`. `subscription_opportunity_cost()` puts a price on recurring charges by showing what the money would grow to if invested. Together they cover the recording side of personal finance, which feeds the allocation decisions in [Budgeting](03-budgeting.qmd).

* [Tracking Spending](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/tracking_spending.html) in Personal Finance: a field manual
* Reference: `apply_rules()`, `subscription_opportunity_cost()`, `percent_of_income()`
* Next: [Budgeting](03-budgeting.qmd)


### Budgeting

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import polars as pl
from perfinpy import *
```

Most budgeting decisions come down to a handful of small calculations. You need to know how big a slice of your paycheck an expense takes and what a daily habit costs over a year. You also need to know what money spent today could have grown into, and how long an upfront purchase takes to pay for itself. The [Budgeting](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/budgeting.html) chapter of the book builds each of these from scratch. In this page I'll answer the same questions with `percent_of_income()`, `to_annual()`, `to_monthly()`, `opportunity_cost()`, and `months_to_break_even()`, using the chapter's numbers so you can check every result against the book.

## The budgeting functions

All five functions accept arrays, and they follow the conventions in [Get started](00-get-started.qmd): rates go in as decimals and ratios come out as percents.

| Function | Returns | Units |
|---|---|---|
| `percent_of_income()` | an expense as a share of income | percent (`30` is 30%) |
| `to_annual()` | a daily, weekly, or monthly amount per year | dollars per year |
| `to_monthly()` | a daily, weekly, or annual amount per month | dollars per month |
| `opportunity_cost()` | what an amount could grow to if invested | dollars (`rate` is a decimal) |
| `months_to_break_even()` | months until savings cover an upfront cost | months, not rounded |

## What share of income does an expense take?

The chapter's first job example takes home \$3,200 a month and pays \$960 in rent. The question is how much of that paycheck rent claims.

Think of the monthly take home pay as a single bar. Rent is one slice of it, and the rest of the bar is what's left for everything else:

![Rent (\$960) as a share of \$3,200 take home pay](assets/budgeting-pct-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Bar model: one horizontal bar for $3,200 of monthly take home pay, split into a vermillion slice labeled Rent $960 and a bluish green slice labeled Remaining $2,240. The rent slice covers just under a third of the bar."}

`percent_of_income()` divides the width of the slice by the width of the whole bar, then multiplies by 100:

```{python}
#| label: rent-share
rent_share = percent_of_income(expense=960, income=3200)
rent_share
```

Rent takes `{python} f"{rent_share:g}"`% of take home pay. The result is a percent, not a decimal, so `30` means 30% (see the conventions table in [Get started](00-get-started.qmd)). The expense and the income need to cover the same period. A monthly rent against a yearly salary gives a share that is off by a factor of 12.

## What does a small habit cost over a year?

A \$5 daily coffee doesn't feel expensive, because you only ever pay \$5 at a time. The same habit looks very different at longer time scales:

![The same \$5 a day habit across four time periods](assets/budgeting-annual-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Bar chart of the same $5 a day coffee habit at four time scales: daily $5, weekly $35, monthly $152, and annual $1,825. The annual bar towers over the other three, which barely rise above zero."}

Each bar is the one before it scaled by the number of periods it contains. `to_annual()` makes the daily to yearly jump in one step:

```{python}
#| label: coffee-annual
coffee_year = to_annual(amount=5, period="daily")
coffee_year
```

The coffee habit costs \$`{python} f"{coffee_year:,.0f}"` a year. Suddenly it's a real number you can evaluate.

### Most budgets work in months

`to_monthly()` goes in the other direction. It converts a daily, weekly, or annual amount to a monthly one, which is the unit most budgets use. Here is the coffee habit per month:

```{python}
#| label: coffee-monthly
coffee_month = to_monthly(amount=5, period="daily")
coffee_month
```

Coffee runs \$`{python} f"{coffee_month:,.2f}"` a month, which matches the monthly bar above. The chapter's second example converts \$150 a week in groceries to a monthly amount:

```{python}
#| label: groceries-monthly
groceries_month = to_monthly(amount=150, period="weekly")
groceries_month
```

Groceries come to \$`{python} f"{groceries_month:,.2f}"` a month. That is more than four weeks' worth, because a month holds about 4.33 weeks.

## What could the money have become?

The chapter frames opportunity cost with a car. Buying a used one for \$15,000 instead of a new one for \$40,000 frees up \$25,000, which the chapter invests at 7% a year. Every dollar spent isn't just that dollar; it's what that dollar could have become.

![\$25,000 invested at 7%: value at each checkpoint](assets/budgeting-opp-cost-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Bar chart of $25,000 invested at 7% a year, with bluish green bars at year 0 ($25,000), year 5 ($35,064), year 10 ($49,179), year 20 ($96,742), and year 30 ($190,306). Each bar is taller than the last, and the gaps between them widen over time."}

Each year multiplies the previous bar by 1.07. `opportunity_cost()` compounds the amount over the full horizon, with the rate as a decimal:

```{python}
#| label: car-gap
car_gap = opportunity_cost(amount=25000, rate=0.07, years=30)
car_gap
```

After 30 years, the \$25,000 gap grows to about \$`{python} f"{car_gap:,.0f}"`. That's not a car payment difference; that's a retirement chapter.

## When does an upfront cost pay for itself?

Some purchases cost money now to save money later: a membership, a better phone plan, or a used bike for commuting. The chapter's example is a \$500 membership that saves \$60 a month.

![\$60 a month in savings accumulating toward a \$500 upfront cost](assets/budgeting-break-even-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Bar chart of cumulative savings at $60 a month over 10 months, rising from $60 in month 1 to $600 in month 10, with a dashed vermillion line marking the $500 upfront cost. Months 1 through 8 are bluish green and sit below the line; months 9 and 10 are blue and rise above it."}

Each month the cumulative savings bar grows by \$60, and break even is the first month that bar crosses the \$500 line. `months_to_break_even()` divides the upfront cost by the monthly savings:

```{python}
#| label: membership
import math

be_months = months_to_break_even(upfront_cost=500, monthly_savings=60)
be_months
```

The membership pays for itself after `{python} f"{be_months:.1f}"` months. The result isn't rounded. Use `math.ceil()` to find the first whole month you come out ahead: month `{python} math.ceil(be_months)`, the first bar above the line in the bar model. If you'll keep the membership longer than that, it's worth the upfront cost.

## Variations

Array inputs let one call answer several versions of the same question. The chapter's periodic expenses are a good example. Setting aside one twelfth of each annual cost every month builds a sinking fund (money saved each month for a known future expense). `to_monthly()` converts every expense at once:

```{python}
#| label: sinking-funds
sinking = pl.DataFrame({
    "expense": ["car insurance", "gifts", "car maintenance", "vacation"],
    "annual": [1200, 600, 1200, 2400],
})
sinking = sinking.with_columns(
    monthly=to_monthly(amount=sinking["annual"].to_numpy(), period="annual")
)
sinking
```

Together these periodic expenses need \$`{python} f"{sinking['monthly'].sum():,.0f}"` a month. When a bill arrives, the money is already there.

### One call compares every time horizon

The same approach works for time horizons. Passing several values to `years` reproduces each checkpoint in the car bar model:

```{python}
#| label: car-gap-horizons
horizons = [0, 5, 10, 20, 30]
pl.DataFrame({
    "years": horizons,
    "value": opportunity_cost(amount=25000, rate=0.07, years=horizons),
})
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
`to_monthly()` uses rounded factors (30.44 days and 4.33 weeks per month), while `to_annual()` uses 365 days and 52 weeks per year. A round trip through both functions drifts slightly. The weekly grocery bill gives a different yearly total depending on the path:

```{python}
#| label: round-trip
(
    to_annual(amount=150, period="weekly"),
    to_annual(amount=groceries_month, period="monthly"),
)
```

A few other limits apply:

* `to_annual()` accepts `"daily"`, `"weekly"`, or `"monthly"`, and `to_monthly()` accepts `"daily"`, `"weekly"`, or `"annual"`. Any other `period` raises a `ValueError`.
* `opportunity_cost()` assumes the same return every year and ignores inflation, taxes, and fund fees.
* `months_to_break_even()` assumes the savings are the same every month and ignores what the upfront cost could have earned if invested.
* `percent_of_income()` and `months_to_break_even()` raise a `ValueError` when `income` or `monthly_savings` is zero or negative.
:::

## Putting it together
