Both investors put in the same \$`{python} f"{300 * 12 * 40:,.0f}"`. The 1% fee cost \$`{python} f"{index_fund - active_fund:,.0f}"`, about `{python} f"{(index_fund - active_fund) / index_fund * 100:.0f}"`% of what the index fund investor ended up with.

## Variations

Passing several horizons to `years` reproduces every pair of bars in the bar model in one call per fund:

```{python}
#| label: fee-drag-horizons
years = [10, 20, 30, 40]
fee_drag = pl.DataFrame({
    "years": years,
    "index_fund": future_value_after_fees(300, 0.07, 0.0004, years),
    "active_fund": future_value_after_fees(300, 0.07, 0.01, years),
}).with_columns(cost_of_fees=pl.col("index_fund") - pl.col("active_fund"))
fee_drag
```

The cost of the fee grows faster than the balances do, because the money it takes would have compounded too.

### Comparing expense ratios

The chapter suggests looking for funds under 0.10%. Passing a range of expense ratios shows what each one leaves after 40 years:

```{python}
#| label: fee-ratios
ratios = [0.0003, 0.0004, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01]
pl.DataFrame({
    "expense_ratio": ratios,
    "fee_on_10k": yearly_fee(balance=10000, expense_ratio=ratios),
    "after_40_years": future_value_after_fees(300, 0.07, ratios, 40),
})
```

The difference between 0.03% and 0.10% is small. The difference between 0.10% and 1% is not.

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
A few things these functions leave out:

* `yearly_fee()` uses one balance. A fund charges its fee on your balance through the year, so a growing account pays a little more than this.
* `future_value_after_fees()` subtracts the expense ratio from the return and assumes both stay the same every year. Contributions are monthly, made at the end of each month.
* Neither function counts sales charges (loads), trading costs, advisor fees, or taxes in a taxable account.
:::

## Putting it together

The 0.04% fee looks harmless at \$4 a year, but it's charged on the balance, and the balance gets large. `yearly_fee()` shows what each fund charges in year 40, using each fund's own ending balance:

```{python}
#| label: fee-year-40
fees_40 = yearly_fee(balance=[index_fund, active_fund], expense_ratio=[0.0004, 0.01])
fees_40
```

In the last year alone, the active fund takes \$`{python} f"{fees_40[1]:,.0f}"` while the index fund takes \$`{python} f"{fees_40[0]:,.0f}"`.

With an expense ratio of 0, `future_value_after_fees()` gives the same answer as `future_value_series()` from [Investing Basics](09-investing-basics.qmd). Comparing the fee free number with the index fund shows how little a low fee costs:

```{python}
#| label: no-fee
no_fee = future_value_series(contribution=300, rate=0.07 / 12, periods=40 * 12)
no_fee, no_fee - index_fund
```

A 0.04% fee costs about \$`{python} f"{no_fee - index_fund:,.0f}"` over 40 years, compared with \$`{python} f"{index_fund - active_fund:,.0f}"` for a 1% fee.

## Recap

Fees are the one part of investing you control. `yearly_fee()` turns an expense ratio into dollars for one year, and `future_value_after_fees()` shows what that fee costs over a working lifetime. A 1% fee can cost close to a quarter of your money, so look for broad index funds that charge under 0.10%.

* [Index Funds](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/index_funds.html) in Personal Finance: a field manual
* Reference: `yearly_fee()`, `future_value_after_fees()`
* Next: [Asset Allocation](12-asset-allocation.qmd)


### Asset Allocation

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import polars as pl
from perfinpy import *
```

Your asset allocation is how you split your investments between stocks and bonds. It does more to decide how your money grows (and how bumpy the ride feels) than which funds you pick. Asset allocation math answers two questions. What does a split do in a good year and a bad year? And how much do you move when you rebalance? In this page I'll answer both with `portfolio_return()` and `rebalance_amount()`, using the numbers from the [Asset Allocation](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/asset_allocation.html) chapter of the book.

## The asset allocation functions

Both functions accept arrays and follow the conventions in [Get started](00-get-started.qmd): shares and returns are decimals. `portfolio_return()` also accepts polars expressions, so it works inside `with_columns()`.

| Function | Returns | Units |
|---|---|---|
| `portfolio_return()` | the return on a stock and bond split | decimal (`-0.32` is a 32% loss) |
| `rebalance_amount()` | how much to buy or sell to reach a target | dollars (positive buys, negative sells) |

## What does a split do in good and bad years?

The chapter splits \$10,000 three ways: 100/0, 80/20, and 60/40 (stocks/bonds). It assumes stocks earn 10% in an average year and lose 40% in a bad year. Bonds earn 4% in an average year and break even in a bad year. These are round numbers for illustration, not predictions.

![\$10,000 in an average year and a bad year, by stock/bond split](assets/asset-allocation-mix-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Bar chart of the change in $10,000 for three stock/bond splits, with a green bar for an average year and a vermillion bar for a bad year. The average year gains are $1,000 for 100/0, $880 for 80/20, and $760 for 60/40. The bad year losses are $4,000, $3,200, and $2,400. Adding bonds shrinks the gains a little and the losses a lot."}

Each bar is a weighted average: the stock return times the share in stocks, plus the bond return times the share in bonds. `portfolio_return()` takes the share in stocks and the two returns. Here is the 80/20 split in a bad year and an average year:

```{python}
#| label: mix-80-20
bad_80 = portfolio_return(stock_pct=0.80, stock_return=-0.40, bond_return=0.0)
avg_80 = portfolio_return(stock_pct=0.80, stock_return=0.10, bond_return=0.04)
bad_80, avg_80
```

In a bad year the 80/20 split loses `{python} f"{-bad_80 * 100:.0f}"`%, or \$`{python} f"{-bad_80 * 10000:,.0f}"` on \$10,000. In an average year it gains `{python} f"{avg_80 * 100:.1f}"`%, or \$`{python} f"{avg_80 * 10000:,.0f}"`. The result is a decimal, so multiply by the balance to get dollars.

## How much do you move when you rebalance?

Your split won't stay where you set it. The chapter starts with \$10,000 at 80/20 (\$8,000 in stocks and \$2,000 in bonds), then stocks drop 30%. The stock part of the bar shrinks to \$5,600, the total falls to \$7,600, and stocks are now only about 74% of it.

![An 80/20 portfolio before a 30% stock drop, after it, and after rebalancing](assets/asset-allocation-rebalance-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Horizontal stacked bar chart of a portfolio at three stages, with stocks in dark green and bonds in light green. Before the drop it holds $8,000 in stocks and $2,000 in bonds. After the drop it holds $5,600 and $2,000. After rebalancing the total is still $7,600, split $6,080 in stocks and $1,520 in bonds."}

Rebalancing moves just enough from bonds to stocks to get back to 80/20. The target for stocks is 80% of the new total, and `rebalance_amount()` returns the difference between that target and what you hold:

```{python}
#| label: rebalance-stocks
move = rebalance_amount(target_pct=0.80, total=5600 + 2000, current_amount=5600)
move
```

A positive answer means buy. You move \$`{python} f"{move:,.0f}"` from bonds into stocks, which means buying stocks while they're down. That's exactly what rebalancing is for.

## Variations

The chapter's Python code builds all three splits at once with polars. Because `portfolio_return()` accepts `pl.col("stocks")`, it works inside `with_columns()` like any other expression. Multiplying by the \$10,000 balance gives the dollar labels from the bar model:

```{python}
#| label: mix-polars
pl.DataFrame({"stocks": [1.0, 0.8, 0.6]}).with_columns(
    average=portfolio_return(pl.col("stocks"), 0.10, 0.04),
    bad=portfolio_return(pl.col("stocks"), -0.40, 0.0),
).with_columns(
    average_dollars=pl.col("average") * 10000,
    bad_dollars=pl.col("bad") * 10000,
)
```

Moving from 100/0 to 60/40 gives up \$240 in an average year and saves \$1,600 in a bad one.

### Rebalancing every fund at once

`rebalance_amount()` takes arrays, so one call rebalances every fund in a portfolio. Suppose the chapter's three fund portfolio (60% US stocks, 30% international stocks, 10% bonds) has drifted to \$6,600, \$2,500, and \$900:

```{python}
#| label: rebalance-three-fund
current = [6600, 2500, 900]
pl.DataFrame({
    "fund": ["US stocks", "international stocks", "bonds"],
    "target_pct": [0.60, 0.30, 0.10],
    "current": current,
    "move": rebalance_amount(
        target_pct=[0.60, 0.30, 0.10], total=sum(current), current_amount=current
    ),
})
```

Sell \$600 of US stocks and use it to buy the other two. The moves add up to zero, because rebalancing only shifts money between funds.

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
Both functions are simple on purpose:

* `portfolio_return()` covers two assets (stocks and bonds) for one year. The returns you pass are assumptions, and it ignores fees, taxes, and inflation.
* `rebalance_amount()` doesn't check that your targets add up to 100%, and `total` has to include `current_amount`.
* `rebalance_amount()` ignores trading costs and the taxes that selling can trigger in a taxable account. Inside a 401(k) or IRA, selling doesn't trigger taxes.
:::

## Putting it together

Here is the chapter's bad year from start to finish. \$10,000 at 80/20 meets a 30% stock drop, and bonds break even. `portfolio_return()` gives the loss on the whole portfolio, and `rebalance_amount()` gives the move:

```{python}
#| label: drop-and-rebalance
drop = portfolio_return(stock_pct=0.80, stock_return=-0.30, bond_return=0.0)
after_drop = 10000 * (1 + drop)
to_stocks = rebalance_amount(
    target_pct=0.80, total=after_drop, current_amount=8000 * (1 - 0.30)
)
drop, after_drop, to_stocks
```

The portfolio falls `{python} f"{-drop * 100:.0f}"`% to \$`{python} f"{after_drop:,.0f}"`, and rebalancing moves \$`{python} f"{to_stocks:,.0f}"` into stocks. How long until it's back to \$10,000? If the next years are average ones, the 80/20 split grows at `{python} f"{avg_80 * 100:.1f}"`% a year, and `future_value()` from [Investing Basics](09-investing-basics.qmd) shows the path:

```{python}
#| label: recovery
recovery_years = [1, 2, 3, 4]
pl.DataFrame({
    "years": recovery_years,
    "value": future_value(present_value=after_drop, rate=avg_80, years=recovery_years),
})
```

The portfolio is back above \$10,000 in year 4. Staying invested (and rebalancing into the drop) is what makes the recovery possible.

## Recap

Asset allocation is how you split your money between stocks and bonds, and it matters more than which funds you pick. `portfolio_return()` shows what a split does in a good year and a bad one, and it works on polars columns as well as numbers. `rebalance_amount()` shows how much to move to get back on target, which makes you buy low without predicting anything.

* [Asset Allocation](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/asset_allocation.html) in Personal Finance: a field manual
* Reference: `portfolio_return()`, `rebalance_amount()`
* Next: [Taxes](13-taxes.qmd)



## Taxes and insurance

### Taxes

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import polars as pl
from perfinpy import *
```

Taxes are the biggest bill most people pay, and two questions come up again and again. How much federal income tax do you owe on your salary? And how much of a raise do you keep once a higher bracket takes its share? The [Taxes](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/taxes.html) chapter of the book answers both by slicing income into brackets. In this page I'll answer the same questions with `income_tax()` and `raise_kept()`, using the chapter's numbers so you can check every result against the book.

## The tax functions

Both functions take single numbers only (see the conventions table in [Get started](00-get-started.qmd)). To compare several incomes, loop over them; the Variations section shows how.

| Function | Returns | Units |
|---|---|---|
| `income_tax()` | 2026 federal income tax for a single filer | dollars per year |
| `raise_kept()` | the part of a raise left after federal income tax | dollars per year |

## How much tax do you owe on a salary?

The chapter's example is a \$45,000 salary for a single filer in 2026. The question is the federal income tax bill, and what share of the salary it takes.

Think of the salary as one long bar. The first \$16,100 is covered by the standard deduction and isn't taxed. The next \$12,400 is taxed at 10%. The last \$16,500 is taxed at 12%:

![A \$45,000 salary, sliced by the standard deduction and 2026 tax brackets](assets/taxes-bracket-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Stacked horizontal bar of a $45,000 salary split into three slices. A pale green slice of $16,100 for the standard deduction owes $0 tax, a bluish green slice of $12,400 in the 10% bracket owes $1,240, and a blue slice of $16,500 in the 12% bracket owes $1,980. Only the last slice is taxed at the top rate."}

`income_tax()` subtracts the deduction, multiplies each slice by its own rate, and adds up the slices:

```{python}
#| label: salary-tax
tax = income_tax(income=45000)
effective = tax / 45000
tax, effective
```

The tax is \$`{python} f"{tax:,.0f}"`, an effective rate of `{python} f"{effective * 100:.1f}"`%. That is well below 12%, the marginal rate on this salary's last dollar. The effective rate is a decimal here because we divided it ourselves; `income_tax()` returns dollars, not a rate.

## How much of a raise do you keep?

Now imagine you earn \$66,000 and get a \$2,000 raise. Taxable income goes from \$49,900 to \$51,900, which crosses the 22% line at \$50,400. The fear is that the higher bracket eats the raise.

The bar below is just the raise. The first \$500 fills the rest of the 12% bracket, and only the last \$1,500 is taxed at 22%:

![A \$2,000 raise that crosses into the 22% bracket](assets/taxes-raise-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Stacked horizontal bar of a $2,000 raise split into three parts. A long bluish green slice labeled You keep $1,610 fills most of the bar, a thin pale green slice is $60 of tax at 12%, and a vermillion slice is $330 of tax at 22%. Most of the raise stays with you even after crossing into the higher bracket."}

`raise_kept()` takes the tax on the new income, subtracts the tax on the old income, and takes that difference out of the raise:

```{python}
#| label: raise
kept = raise_kept(old_income=66000, raise_amount=2000)
extra_tax = income_tax(income=68000) - income_tax(income=66000)
kept, extra_tax
```

You keep \$`{python} f"{kept:,.0f}"` of the \$2,000 raise, and the extra tax is \$`{python} f"{extra_tax:,.0f}"`. Crossing into a higher bracket never makes a raise cost you money; only the dollars above the line pay the higher rate.

## The call stack

`raise_kept()` doesn't have its own bracket table. It calls `income_tax()` twice, once on the new income and once on the old income, and subtracts the two results. The tree below shows that relationship:

```{python}
#| label: call-stack
#| eval: false
from rich import print
from rich.tree import Tree

tree = Tree("raise_kept()")
tree.add("income_tax(old_income + raise_amount)")
tree.add("income_tax(old_income)")
print(tree)
```

```
raise_kept()
├── income_tax(old_income + raise_amount)
└── income_tax(old_income)
```

Any change to the brackets in `income_tax()` flows straight into `raise_kept()`.

## Variations

Because both functions take single numbers, a list comprehension compares several salaries. The table below puts the tax and the effective rate side by side:

```{python}
#| label: incomes
incomes = [30000, 45000, 66000, 100000, 150000]
taxes = [income_tax(income=i) for i in incomes]
pl.DataFrame({
    "income": incomes,
    "tax": taxes,
    "effective_rate": [t / i for t, i in zip(taxes, incomes)],
})
```

The effective rate climbs with income, but it stays below each salary's top bracket. The same pattern works for raises. Here is a \$2,000 raise at each salary:

```{python}
#| label: raises
pl.DataFrame({
    "income": incomes,
    "kept": [raise_kept(old_income=i, raise_amount=2000) for i in incomes],
})
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
`income_tax()` hard codes the 2026 federal brackets for a single filer and a \$16,100 standard deduction. A few other limits apply:

* Other years, married filers, and heads of household need different brackets, which the function doesn't take.
* You can pass a different `deduction` (for example, itemized deductions), but not different brackets.
* Neither function counts credits, FICA (7.65%), state or local taxes, or self employment tax.
* Both functions take single numbers only. A list or array raises a `ValueError`; text raises a `TypeError`.
:::

## Putting it together

Back to the \$45,000 salary. Federal income tax is only part of what comes out of the paycheck. FICA (Social Security and Medicare) takes 7.65% of every dollar, with no deduction. `percent_of_income()` from the [Budgeting](03-budgeting.qmd) page shows how much of the salary the two together claim:

```{python}
#| label: paycheck
salary = 45000
fica = salary * 0.0765
federal = income_tax(income=salary)
total = fica + federal
total_share = percent_of_income(expense=total, income=salary)
fica, federal, total_share
```

FICA takes \$`{python} f"{fica:,.2f}"` and federal income tax takes \$`{python} f"{federal:,.0f}"`. Together they claim `{python} f"{total_share:.1f}"`% of the salary, before any state tax.

Next, a \$2,000 raise on the same salary. All of it stays in the 12% bracket, so you keep a little more than in the \$66,000 example:

```{python}
#| label: raise-45k
raise_kept(old_income=salary, raise_amount=2000)
```

This number is before FICA, which takes another 7.65% of the raise.

## Recap

Tax brackets apply to slices of income, not the whole salary. `income_tax()` adds up the tax on each slice, and dividing by income gives the effective rate. `raise_kept()` calls `income_tax()` twice to show that a raise always leaves you with more money.

* [Taxes](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/taxes.html) in Personal Finance: a field manual
* Reference: `income_tax()`, `raise_kept()`
* Next: [Insurance](14-insurance.qmd)


### Insurance

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import polars as pl
from perfinpy import *
```

Insurance math helps with two everyday choices. Which deductible should you pick, and which health plan costs less over a year? The [Insurance](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/insurance.html) chapter of the book answers both with a little arithmetic. In this page I'll answer the same questions with `break_even_years()` and `plan_cost()`, using the chapter's numbers so you can check every result against the book.

## The insurance functions

Both functions accept arrays, so one call can compare several deductibles or several kinds of years.

| Function | Returns | Units |
|---|---|---|
| `break_even_years()` | years of premium savings needed to cover a higher deductible | years, not rounded |
| `plan_cost()` | the yearly cost of a health plan | dollars per year |

## Which deductible should you pick?

The chapter's car insurance costs \$1,500 a year with a \$500 deductible, or \$1,350 a year with a \$1,000 deductible. The higher deductible saves \$150 a year, but you pay \$500 more each time you file a claim.

Each bar below is the savings piling up year after year. The dashed line is the extra \$500 you'd pay on a claim:

![Savings from a \$1,000 deductible vs. a \$500 deductible, year by year](assets/insurance-deductible-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Bar chart of cumulative premium savings over five years: $150, $300, $450, $600, and $750. A dashed vermillion line at $500 is labeled Extra $500 per claim. Years 1 to 3 are bluish green and sit below the line; years 4 and 5 are blue and rise above it, so the savings pass the extra deductible a little after year 3."}

`break_even_years()` divides the gap between the deductibles by the yearly savings:

```{python}
#| label: deductible
years = break_even_years(high_deductible=1000, low_deductible=500, yearly_savings=150)
years
```

The savings cover the extra deductible after about `{python} f"{years:.1f}"` years. If you go longer than that between claims, the higher deductible comes out ahead. Most drivers go much longer, but pick it only if your emergency fund can cover the \$1,000.

## Which health plan costs less?

Your job offers two plans. Plan A has a \$100 monthly premium and a \$3,000 out of pocket maximum. Plan B is a high deductible plan with a \$40 monthly premium, a \$5,000 out of pocket maximum, and \$500 a year from your employer into your HSA. We'll compare a healthy year (about \$300 of care) with the worst year possible.

![Total yearly cost of two health plans in a healthy year and the worst year](assets/insurance-health-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Grouped bar chart of yearly health plan cost in two kinds of year. In a healthy year, Plan A (bluish green) costs $1,500 and Plan B (blue) costs $280. In the worst year, Plan A costs $4,200 and Plan B costs $4,980. Plan B is far cheaper in a healthy year and somewhat more expensive in the worst year."}

Each bar is twelve premiums, plus your medical bills up to the out of pocket maximum, minus the employer's HSA money. `plan_cost()` takes `float("inf")` for `medical_cost` to get the worst year, because the bills are then capped at the maximum:

```{python}
#| label: plans
costs = [300, float("inf")]
plan_a = plan_cost(monthly_premium=100, medical_cost=costs, oop_max=3000)
plan_b = plan_cost(monthly_premium=40, medical_cost=costs, oop_max=5000, employer_hsa=500)
pl.DataFrame({"year": ["healthy", "worst"], "plan_a": plan_a, "plan_b": plan_b})
```

Plan B saves \$`{python} f"{plan_a[0] - plan_b[0]:,.0f}"` in a healthy year and costs \$`{python} f"{plan_b[1] - plan_a[1]:,.0f}"` more in the worst year. The worst year is the ceiling on what each plan can cost you.

## Variations

The deductible decision depends on how much the higher deductible saves. Passing several values to `yearly_savings` shows how fast each one breaks even:

```{python}
#| label: savings-options
savings = [100, 150, 250]
pl.DataFrame({
    "yearly_savings": savings,
    "years": break_even_years(high_deductible=1000, low_deductible=500, yearly_savings=savings),
})
```

The bigger the yearly savings, the sooner the higher deductible pays off.

### Health plans across many kinds of year

Most years fall somewhere between healthy and worst. One call per plan covers a range of medical bills:

```{python}
#| label: bill-range
bills = [0.0, 300.0, 1000.0, 2500.0, 5000.0, float("inf")]
pl.DataFrame({
    "medical_cost": bills,
    "plan_a": plan_cost(monthly_premium=100, medical_cost=bills, oop_max=3000),
    "plan_b": plan_cost(monthly_premium=40, medical_cost=bills, oop_max=5000, employer_hsa=500),
})
```

With no medical bills at all, Plan B's cost is negative: the employer's \$500 is more than the \$480 of premiums. Plan B stays cheaper until the bills pass about \$4,220. Past that point Plan A has hit its maximum, and it comes out ahead.

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
Both functions use the simple version of the math in the chapter. A few limits apply:

* `plan_cost()` assumes you pay every medical bill up to the out of pocket maximum. For plans with coinsurance, it slightly overstates the cost.
* `plan_cost()` ignores copays, tax savings from HSA contributions, and what HSA money could earn if invested.
* `break_even_years()` assumes the premium savings are the same every year and ignores premium increases after a claim.
* `break_even_years()` raises a `ValueError` when `yearly_savings` is zero or negative. Text raises a `TypeError`, and `nan` raises a `ValueError` in either function.
:::

## Putting it together

The chapter suggests putting Plan B's healthy year savings into the HSA. How many healthy years does it take for those savings to cover Plan B's extra cost in a worst year? The structure is the same as the deductible question: a gap divided by savings per year. That means `break_even_years()` answers it too:

```{python}
#| label: hsa-cushion
cushion = break_even_years(
    high_deductible=plan_b[1],
    low_deductible=plan_a[1],
    yearly_savings=plan_a[0] - plan_b[0],
)
cushion
```

The savings cover the worst year gap in `{python} f"{cushion:.2f}"` years, so a single healthy year is enough. After that, a bad year on Plan B still leaves you ahead of Plan A overall. The same rule as the deductible applies: have an emergency fund that covers the \$5,000 maximum first (see [Emergency Fund](05-emergency-fund.qmd)).

## Recap

Insurance choices trade a known cost now for a possible cost later. `break_even_years()` shows how long the premium savings take to cover a higher deductible. `plan_cost()` puts two health plans on the same yearly scale, from a healthy year to the worst one.

* [Insurance](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/insurance.html) in Personal Finance: a field manual
* Reference: `break_even_years()`, `plan_cost()`
* Next: [Financial Goals](15-financial-goals.qmd)



## Planning

### Financial Goals

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import polars as pl
from perfinpy import *
```

A goal without a number and a date is a wish. Once you have both, two questions are left: how much do you set aside each month, and which goal do you fund first when you can't fund them all? In this page I'll answer both with `monthly_for_goal()` and `months_to_fund()`, using the numbers from the [Financial Goals](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/financial_goals.html) chapter of the book so you can check every result.

## The goal functions

Both functions accept arrays and follow the conventions on the [Get started](00-get-started.qmd) page.

| Function | Returns | Units |
|---|---|---|
| `monthly_for_goal()` | the monthly deposit that grows into a goal | dollars per month (`annual_rate` is a decimal) |
| `months_to_fund()` | months to save a goal with no interest | whole months, rounded up (an `int`) |

## How much should you save each month?

The chapter's example is a \$15,000 down payment in five years. The money sits in a high yield savings account earning 4% a year. Without interest you would divide \$15,000 by 60 months and save \$250 a month. Interest does part of the work, so you can save a little less.

The bar below is the \$15,000 goal. Most of it comes from your deposits, and interest fills in the rest:

![A \$15,000 goal in 5 years at 4%: your deposits plus interest](assets/financial-goals-goal-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Bar model: one horizontal bar for a $15,000 goal, split into a long bluish green section labeled Your deposits $13,575 and a short blue section labeled Interest $1,425. Deposits cover about nine tenths of the bar; interest covers the last tenth."}

`monthly_for_goal()` works backward from the future value of a series of deposits. It asks which monthly deposit grows into the goal, compounding at `annual_rate / 12`:

```{python}
#| label: goal-monthly
monthly = monthly_for_goal(goal=15000, annual_rate=0.04, months=60)
monthly
```

You need about \$`{python} f"{monthly:,.2f}"` a month, which is \$`{python} f"{250 - monthly:,.2f}"` less than saving without interest. Over five years your deposits total \$`{python} f"{monthly * 60:,.0f}"`, and interest adds the other \$`{python} f"{15000 - monthly * 60:,.0f}"`.

## Which goal comes first?

Say you can save \$600 a month toward two goals: a \$3,000 trip and a \$9,000 car. You can fund them one at a time (trip first, then car), or split the \$600 evenly until the trip is paid for and then send everything to the car.

Each bar below is a goal on a timeline. It starts at month 0 and ends the month the goal is fully funded:

![Two goals funded with \$600 a month: one at a time vs. split evenly](assets/financial-goals-sequence-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Grouped horizontal bar chart of months to fund two goals under two plans. One at a time: the light green trip bar ends at month 5 and the bluish green car bar ends at month 20. Split evenly: the trip bar ends at month 10 and the car bar ends at month 20. The car finishes at month 20 under both plans."}

`months_to_fund()` divides the goal by the monthly amount going to it and rounds up to a whole month. The last goal is done when all of the money is saved, so its goal is the total of both:

```{python}
#| label: goal-sequence
one_at_a_time = (
    months_to_fund(goal=3000, monthly=600),
    months_to_fund(goal=3000 + 9000, monthly=600),
)
split_evenly = (
    months_to_fund(goal=3000, monthly=300),
    months_to_fund(goal=3000 + 9000, monthly=600),
)
one_at_a_time, split_evenly
```

The trip finishes at month `{python} one_at_a_time[0]` one at a time, or month `{python} split_evenly[0]` split evenly. The car finishes at month `{python} one_at_a_time[1]` either way. The order only decides which goal you get first.

## Variations

Passing several rates to `annual_rate` shows how much interest helps the down payment goal. The 0% row is the plain \$15,000 ÷ 60:

```{python}
#| label: goal-rates
rates = [0.0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.05]
pl.DataFrame({
    "annual_rate": rates,
    "monthly": monthly_for_goal(goal=15000, annual_rate=rates, months=60),
})
```

Each point of interest trims the deposit by a few dollars a month. Time matters more. The same goal over three, five, and seven years:

```{python}
#| label: goal-horizons
months = [36, 60, 84]
pl.DataFrame({
    "months": months,
    "monthly": monthly_for_goal(goal=15000, annual_rate=0.04, months=months),
    "months_no_interest": months_to_fund(goal=15000, monthly=[400, 250, 180]),
})
```

The last column runs the other direction: it asks how long \$400, \$250, or \$180 a month takes with no interest at all.

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
`monthly_for_goal()` assumes the same rate every month and a deposit at the end of each month. It ignores taxes on interest and inflation, so a goal priced in today's dollars will cost more later. `months_to_fund()` ignores interest entirely and rounds up, so it gives the first month the goal is fully funded.

Both functions stop with a `ValueError` when the divisor isn't positive:

```{python}
#| label: goal-error
#| error: true
months_to_fund(goal=3000, monthly=0)
```

`monthly_for_goal()` does the same when `months` is 0 or negative.
:::

## Putting it together

Back to the \$600 a month. Suppose the down payment comes first, and whatever is left goes to the trip and the car. The down payment takes the amount we found above, and `months_to_fund()` shows how long the remainder needs for both smaller goals:

```{python}
#| label: goal-together
down_payment = monthly_for_goal(goal=15000, annual_rate=0.04, months=60)
left_over = 600 - down_payment
both_goals = months_to_fund(goal=3000 + 9000, monthly=left_over)
round(left_over, 2), both_goals
```

With \$`{python} f"{left_over:,.2f}"` a month left over, the trip and the car take `{python} both_goals` months instead of 20. That trade is the real decision: the down payment stays on schedule, and the smaller goals wait longer. The [Major Purchases](16-major-purchases.qmd) page picks up the down payment and asks what the mortgage would cost.

## Recap

A goal needs a number, a date, and a monthly amount. `monthly_for_goal()` turns the number and the date into the monthly amount, with interest doing part of the work. `months_to_fund()` shows that the order of your goals changes which one you reach first, but not when the last one is done.

* [Financial Goals](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/financial_goals.html) in Personal Finance: a field manual
* Reference: `monthly_for_goal()`, `months_to_fund()`
* Next: [Major Purchases](16-major-purchases.qmd)


### Major Purchases

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import polars as pl
from perfinpy import *
```

A home is the biggest purchase most people ever make, and small percentages turn into tens of thousands of dollars. The [Major Purchases](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/major_purchases.html) chapter of the book asks three questions: when does renting beat buying, what will the mortgage cost each month, and where does the first payment go? In this page I'll answer them with `rent_buy_threshold()`, `mortgage_payment()`, and `first_payment_split()`, using the chapter's numbers so you can check each result against the book.

## The major purchase functions

`rent_buy_threshold()` and `mortgage_payment()` accept arrays. `first_payment_split()` takes single numbers and returns a `dict`.

| Function | Returns | Units |
|---|---|---|
| `rent_buy_threshold()` | the monthly rent that matches the unrecoverable cost of owning | dollars per month (`unrecoverable_rate` is a decimal, default `0.05`) |
| `mortgage_payment()` | the monthly payment on a fixed rate loan | dollars per month, principal and interest only |
| `first_payment_split()` | the interest and principal in the first payment | a `dict` of dollars, plus `pct_interest` as a percent |

## Should you rent or buy?

Owning a home costs money you never get back, whether or not you have a mortgage. The 5% rule from the chapter adds up three of those costs for a \$500,000 home: about 1% a year for property tax, 1% for maintenance, and 3% for the cost of capital (the return your money could have earned somewhere else).

![The three parts of the 5% rule on a \$500,000 home](assets/major-purchases-rent-buy-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Bar model: one horizontal bar of annual unrecoverable cost on a $500,000 home, split into a vermillion section for property tax (about 1%, $5,000 a year), a bluish green section for maintenance (about 1%, $5,000 a year), and a dark brown section for cost of capital (about 3%, $15,000 a year). The whole bar is $25,000 a year, or $2,083 a month, and cost of capital fills more than half of it."}

`rent_buy_threshold()` takes 5% of the home's value and divides by 12:

```{python}
#| label: rent-buy
threshold = rent_buy_threshold(home_value=500000)
threshold
```

Owning this home costs about \$`{python} f"{threshold:,.0f}"` a month that you never get back. If you can rent a similar place for less than that, renting and investing the difference tends to win.

## What will the mortgage cost each month?

The chapter's loan is \$480,000: a \$600,000 home with 20% down, at 6%. The same loan gives very different payments depending on how many months you spread it over:

![Monthly payment on a \$480,000 loan at 6% across three terms](assets/major-purchases-mortgage-payment-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Bar chart of the monthly payment on a $480,000 loan at 6% for three loan terms: a vermillion bar at $4,051 for 15 years, a bluish green bar at $3,439 for 20 years, and a blue bar at $2,878 for 30 years. Shorter terms have taller bars."}

`mortgage_payment()` spreads the principal plus all future interest into equal monthly payments, with the rate as a decimal:

```{python}
#| label: mortgage
payment = mortgage_payment(principal=480000, annual_rate=0.06, years=30)
payment
```

The 30 year loan costs about \$`{python} f"{payment:,.2f}"` a month. That covers principal and interest only; property tax and insurance come on top.

## Where does the first payment go?

Early mortgage payments are mostly interest. In month one the interest is the full balance times the monthly rate, and only what's left of the payment reduces the principal:

![Interest vs. principal at three points on a \$480,000, 6%, 30 year mortgage](assets/major-purchases-first-payment-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Stacked bar chart of how the same $2,878 monthly payment splits between interest (vermillion) and principal (blue) at three points in a 30 year loan. Month 1: $2,400 interest (83%) and $478 principal (17%). Month 180: $1,711 interest (59%) and $1,167 principal (41%). Month 348: $181 interest (6%) and $2,697 principal (94%). The interest share shrinks as the loan ages."}

`first_payment_split()` returns the payment, its interest and principal parts, and the interest share as a percent:

```{python}
#| label: first-payment
split = first_payment_split(principal=480000, annual_rate=0.06, years=30)
split
```

Of the first \$`{python} f"{split['payment']:,.0f}"` payment, \$`{python} f"{split['interest']:,.0f}"` is interest (`{python} f"{split['pct_interest']:.0f}"`%) and only \$`{python} f"{split['principal']:,.0f}"` reduces the loan. That's why moving after a few years leaves you with very little principal paid down.

### Call stack

`first_payment_split()` doesn't repeat the payment formula. It calls `mortgage_payment()`, which uses the internal `_annuity_factor()` helper (the same one behind `monthly_for_goal()`):

```{python}
#| label: call-stack
#| eval: false
from rich import print
from rich.tree import Tree

tree = Tree("first_payment_split()")
tree.add("mortgage_payment()").add("_annuity_factor()")
print(tree)
```

```
first_payment_split()
└── mortgage_payment()
    └── _annuity_factor()
```

## Variations

Passing several terms to `years` reproduces the three bars in the mortgage bar model. Multiplying each payment by the number of payments shows the total interest over the life of the loan:

```{python}
#| label: mortgage-terms
years = [15, 20, 30]
payments = mortgage_payment(principal=480000, annual_rate=0.06, years=years)
pl.DataFrame({
    "years": years,
    "payment": payments,
    "total_interest": payments * [y * 12 for y in years] - 480000,
})
```

The 30 year loan has the lowest payment and more than twice the interest of the 15 year loan. The same approach compares rent thresholds across home prices:

```{python}
#| label: rent-buy-prices
home_values = [300000, 500000, 700000]
pl.DataFrame({
    "home_value": home_values,
    "threshold": rent_buy_threshold(home_value=home_values),
})
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
`rent_buy_threshold()` is a rule of thumb. The 5% default is an average; set `unrecoverable_rate` if your property tax or maintenance is higher or lower. It ignores home price growth, the costs of buying and selling, and how long you stay.

`mortgage_payment()` assumes a fixed rate and returns principal and interest only, with no property tax, insurance, or PMI. A 0% rate returns `principal / (years * 12)`, and `years` must be greater than 0.

`first_payment_split()` takes single numbers only. An array raises an error:

```{python}
#| label: split-error
#| error: true
first_payment_split(principal=480000, annual_rate=0.06, years=[15, 30])
```
:::

## Putting it together

The chapter's loan comes from a \$600,000 home with 20% down. That's a \$120,000 down payment, the kind of goal the [Financial Goals](15-financial-goals.qmd) page plans for. Here is the whole decision in one cell: the monthly saving for the down payment over 10 years at 4%, the rent threshold for the home, and the mortgage payment once you buy:

```{python}
#| label: purchase-together
home = 600000
save_monthly = monthly_for_goal(goal=home * 0.20, annual_rate=0.04, months=120)
rent_line = rent_buy_threshold(home_value=home)
mortgage = mortgage_payment(principal=home * 0.80, annual_rate=0.06, years=30)
round(save_monthly, 2), round(rent_line, 2), round(mortgage, 2)
```

Saving the down payment takes about \$`{python} f"{save_monthly:,.0f}"` a month for 10 years. Once you buy, the mortgage is \$`{python} f"{mortgage:,.0f}"` a month, and the 5% rule says owning costs about \$`{python} f"{rent_line:,.0f}"` a month that you never get back. If a comparable rental costs less than \$`{python} f"{rent_line:,.0f}"`, renting and investing the down payment is worth a serious look.

## Recap

The 5% rule gives a quick rent or buy test, and `rent_buy_threshold()` turns it into a monthly number. `mortgage_payment()` shows how the term changes the payment, and `first_payment_split()` shows how little of an early payment goes to principal. Run these numbers before you fall in love with a floor plan.

* [Major Purchases](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/major_purchases.html) in Personal Finance: a field manual
* Reference: `rent_buy_threshold()`, `mortgage_payment()`, `first_payment_split()`
* Next: [Estate Planning](17-estate-planning.qmd)


### Estate Planning

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import polars as pl
from perfinpy import *
```

Your estate is everything you own and everything you owe. Estate planning math asks two things about it: what is it worth, and how much of it do your beneficiary forms control? In this page I'll answer both with `net_worth()` and `beneficiary_share()`, using the 25 year old from the [Estate Planning](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/estate_planning.html) chapter of the book so you can check each result.

## The estate functions

Both functions take a `dict` of name to amount, as the book does. A plain list of amounts works too.

| Function | Returns | Units |
|---|---|---|
| `net_worth()` | total assets minus total debts | dollars (a `float`) |
| `beneficiary_share()` | the share of assets with a named beneficiary | a decimal (`0.8875` is 88.75%) |

## What is your estate worth?

The chapter's example is a 25 year old with a 401(k), a Roth IRA, some savings, and a car. On the other side are a car loan and a small credit card balance. The bar model puts what you own on one bar and what you owe on the other:

![Assets, debts, and net worth for a 25 year old](assets/estate-planning-networth-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Bar model with two horizontal bars. What you own: 401(k) $12,000 in bluish green, Roth IRA $6,000 in blue, Savings $8,000 in light green, and Car $9,000 in sky blue, for $35,000 in all. What you owe: Car loan $6,000 in vermillion and Credit card $1,000 in orange, for $7,000. The owe bar is about one fifth the length of the own bar."}

Net worth is the length of the top bar minus the length of the bottom bar. `net_worth()` adds up each `dict` and subtracts:

```{python}
#| label: net-worth
assets = {"401k": 12000, "roth_ira": 6000, "savings": 8000, "car": 9000}
debts = {"car_loan": 6000, "credit_card": 1000}
worth = net_worth(assets, debts)
worth
```

The estate is worth \$`{python} f"{worth:,.0f}"`: \$`{python} f"{sum(assets.values()):,}"` in assets minus \$`{python} f"{sum(debts.values()):,}"` in debts.

## How much do your beneficiary forms control?

Now add life insurance through work. Many employers give free coverage equal to one year of salary, say \$45,000. It isn't part of net worth while you're alive, but it pays out when you die. The bar below shows everything that would pass to someone else, split by what decides who gets it:

![What decides who gets each part of the estate](assets/estate-planning-beneficiary-bar-model.png){fig-alt="Bar model: one horizontal bar for an $80,000 estate, split into a bluish green section for beneficiary forms ($63,000), a light green section for savings with a payable on death designation ($8,000), and a vermillion section for your will or state law ($9,000). The two green sections together fill almost nine tenths of the bar."}

The green sections are decided by forms you fill out online; only the vermillion section depends on a will. `beneficiary_share()` divides the green sections by the whole bar:

```{python}
#| label: beneficiary
with_beneficiary = {
    "401k": 12000,
    "roth_ira": 6000,
    "life_insurance": 45000,
    "savings_pod": 8000,
}
without_beneficiary = {"car": 9000}
share = beneficiary_share(with_beneficiary, without_beneficiary)
share
```

About `{python} f"{share * 100:.0f}"`% of the estate is decided by forms that take minutes to fill out. That's why the book puts beneficiary designations ahead of a will for most young people. Note that the result is a decimal, not a percent.

## Variations

`beneficiary_share()` takes one estate at a time, so a list comprehension compares several. Here is the same estate with fewer forms filed:

```{python}
#| label: beneficiary-scenarios
scenarios = {
    "all forms filed": (with_beneficiary, without_beneficiary),
    "no POD on savings": (
        {"401k": 12000, "roth_ira": 6000, "life_insurance": 45000},
        {"savings": 8000, "car": 9000},
    ),
    "retirement forms only": (
        {"401k": 12000, "roth_ira": 6000},
        {"life_insurance": 45000, "savings": 8000, "car": 9000},
    ),
}
pl.DataFrame({
    "scenario": list(scenarios),
    "share": [beneficiary_share(w, wo) for w, wo in scenarios.values()],
})
```

Skipping the life insurance form costs the most, because it is the largest item. (Most employer life insurance asks for a beneficiary at enrollment; the last row shows what happens if you leave it blank.)

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
`net_worth()` adds the values you give it. It doesn't know what a car is worth next year, so use today's market value, and enter debts as positive balances. It ignores taxes owed on retirement accounts and the costs of probate.

`beneficiary_share()` returns a decimal, unlike the ratio functions that return percents. It ignores joint ownership, which also passes outside a will, and it stops with a `ValueError` when total assets aren't greater than 0:

```{python}
#| label: beneficiary-error
#| error: true
beneficiary_share({}, {"car": 0})
```

Both functions raise a `TypeError` for text and a `ValueError` for missing values.
:::

## Putting it together

Estates change as you save. Five years from now, suppose the retirement accounts grow at 7% a year (with `future_value()` from [Investing Basics](09-investing-basics.qmd)), savings reach \$15,000, the car is paid off and worth \$6,000, and the credit card is cleared:

```{python}
#| label: estate-later
retirement = future_value(present_value=[12000, 6000], rate=0.07, years=5)
assets_later = {
    "401k": retirement[0],
    "roth_ira": retirement[1],
    "savings": 15000,
    "car": 6000,
}
worth_later = net_worth(assets_later, debts={"car_loan": 0, "credit_card": 0})
share_later = beneficiary_share(
    {
        "401k": retirement[0],
        "roth_ira": retirement[1],
        "life_insurance": 45000,
        "savings_pod": 15000,
    },
    {"car": 6000},
)
round(worth_later, 2), round(share_later, 4)
```

Net worth grows to \$`{python} f"{worth_later:,.0f}"`, and the forms now decide `{python} f"{share_later * 100:.0f}"`% of the estate. The bigger the accounts get, the more those ten minute forms matter.

## Recap

`net_worth()` gives the starting number for any estate plan: what you own minus what you owe. `beneficiary_share()` shows how much of that estate passes by beneficiary forms instead of a will. For most young people the answer is most of it, so fill in those forms first.
